شاهد البث المباشر لتلفزيون بي بي سي

هل تتدخل تركيا وباكستان لحماية السعودية أمام هجمات الحوثيين؟. مع تصاعد التوترات بين السعودية والحوثيين، واستمرار الهجمات على مدن السعودية، تطرح التساؤلات حول دور "حلف مكة" في مساعدة السعودية ضد حركة أنصار الله الحوثية، فما هو موقف تركيا وباكستان من التصعيد؟
كيف يساعد الذكاء الاصطناعي على إدارة تخزين واستهلاك الكهرباء في المنزل؟
ما الفرق بين المملكة المتحدة وإنجلترا وبريطانيا؟. المملكة المتحدة تضم أربع دول، إنجلترا وويلز وإسكتلندا وأيرلندا الشمالية، وهذه بعض أبرز المعلومات عنها.

كيف أصبحت المسيرات قادرة على استهداف بعضها؟. أعلن الجيش السوداني مؤخرا عن عدة عمليات إسقاط لطائرات مسيرة صينية الصنع مملوكة لقوات الدعم السريع عبر صواريخ جو - جو أطلقت من مسيرات يملكها الجيش. فماذا نعرف عن تقنيات اعتراض الطائرات المسيرة؟ ولماذا يعد ما حدث في السودان تاريخيا؟
بي بي سي في تعز على خط المواجهة حيث تحاول جماعة أنصار الله السيطرة على المدينة. في زيارة نادرة إلى منطقة النزاع في اليمن، تنتقل بي بي سي إلى الخطوط الأمامية برفقة جنود موالين للحكومة
مخيمات تعج بالجرذان وجروح لا تلتئم: هكذا صارت الأوضاع في غزة. فلسطينيون يتحدثون لبي بي سي عن معاناتهم في غزة في أعقاب الدمار شبه الكامل للبنية التحتية التي يعتمدون عليها.

العراق بعد الانسحاب الأمريكي: من شبح "تنظيم الدولة" إلى معركة سلاح الفصائل. مع استكمال انسحاب القوات الأمريكية من العراق، تدخل البلاد مرحلة جديدة تتداخل فيها تحديات أمنية وسياسية وإقليمية. فبين مخاوف عودة نشاط خلايا تنظيم الدولة الإسلامية، وتصاعد نفوذ الفصائل المسلحة الموالية لإيران، يبرز تحدي حصر السلاح بيَد الدولة وتجنب انجرار العراق إلى صراعات إقليمية أوسع.

وردة المسيح والعندليب: قصة القديسة تريز الطفل يسوع وسر لوحة عبد الحليم حافظ في كنيستها بمصر. تكشف لوحة شكر رخامية نادرة كتبها العندليب الأسمر عبد الحليم حافظ مهداة للقديسة تريز، عن حضورها العميق في قلوب الجميع، وعن امتداد سيرتها الروحية من الغرب إلى الشرق، كما أثارت صورة "زهرة بيضاء" وُضعت على قبر البابا الراحل فرنسيس كثيراً من التساؤلات والتأملات: هل هي تلميح رمزي إلى "وردة المسيح الصغيرة" القديسة تريز الطفل يسوع الوجه الأقدس وتأثيرها على حياته وخدمته البابوية؟ فما قصة هذه القديسة صغيرة السن التي أحبها الجميع؟
من هي فاطمة الزهراء المنصوري، أول امرأة تترأس حكومة المغرب؟. فاطمة الزهراء المنصوري قالت إنها ستبدأ مشاورات داخل حزب الأصالة والمعاصرة ثم مع الأحزاب السياسية من أجل اقتراح تشكيلة الحكومة الجديدة.
بعد أكثر من عقدين في العراق، كيف بدأ الوجود العسكري الأمريكي وكيف انتهى؟. تستكمل الولايات المتحدة انسحابها من العراق وفقاً لجدول زمني تم التوافق عليه مع الحكومة في بغداد قبل عامين.

"قراراتي مرتبطة باحتمال تجدُّد القتال": ماذا يعني أن تُصبح الحرب "الوضع الطبيعي"؟. كيف تتغير الحياة عندما تطول الحرب إلى حد تصبح فيه تفاصيلها اليومية أمراً مألوفاً؟ من غزة والسودان إلى سوريا ولبنان وليبيا، تحكي شهادات أشخاص لبي بي سي، عاشوا الحروب والنزوح عن عالم تغيّر فيه معنى البيت والأمان والعمل والأسرة والمستقبل، وأصبح التخطيط للحياة مرتبطاً دائماً باحتمال عودة القتال.

حبس فريق صحفي كامل يعيد ملف حرية الصحافة في مصر إلى الواجهة محلياً ودولياً. ألقت وزارة الداخلية المصرية القبض على ستة صحفيين، يعتقد أنهم كامل فريق عمل منصة للتحقق من المعلومات والأخبار عبر تطبيقات التواصل الاجتماعي، على خلفية اتهامهم بنشر أخبار مفبركة ومغلوطة وانتمائهم لجماعة الإخوان المسلمين، المصنفة إرهابية في مصر، في حين نفت "متصدقش" هذه الاتهامات عبر بيان نشرته الخميس، وقالت إن أرشيفها يتضمن مئات التصحيحات لمعلومات نشرتها جهات وشخصيات محسوبة على جماعة الإخوان.

ما الذي ينتظر الشباب العائدين بعد الحرب؟. قد تتوقف الحرب، لكن طريق العودة لا يبدأ بالضرورة مع توقف القتال. فكيف يمكن استعادة حياة تركتها خلفك؟ وماذا تعني العودة إلى منزلٍ مدمر، أو أرض ما زالت مهددة بمخلفات الحرب؟

المحرشي في بلا قيود: تعيين فاطمة المنصوري في رئاسة الحكومة يُبين مكانة المرأة في المغرب.. نفى العربي المحرشي عضو مجلس النواب المغربي عن حزب الأصالة والمعاصرة بشدة سعي حزبه للقضاء على الإسلاميين في المغرب، في إشارة لحزب العدالة والتنمية الذي أحرز المرتبة الرابعة في الانتخابات الأخيرة.

المغرب: ما أهم التحديات التي تواجه المنصوري بعد تكليفها بتشكيل الحكومة؟. كلّف العاهل المغربي، محمد السادس، منسقة القيادة الجماعية لحزب الأصالة والمعاصرة، فاطمة الزهراء المنصوري، بتشكيل الحكومة الجديدة، بعد تصدر حزبها الانتخابات التشريعية، لتصبح أول امرأة تتولى هذه المهمة في تاريخ المغرب.

بريطانيا تعتقل مواطناً من أصل إيراني على خلفية حادثة قاعدة "فيرفورد" الجوية. قالت فيكي إيفانز، المنسقة الوطنية الأولى لشرطة مكافحة الإرهاب في بريطانيا، إن المحققين يدرسون "جميع الاحتمالات الممكنة، بما في ذلك احتمال تورط دولة أجنبية".
حرائق واحتجاجات طلابية: ماذا يحدث في فرنسا؟. الحكومة الفرنسية تعقد اجتماعاً طارئاً مع تزايد المظاهرات وتحولها إلى أعمال عنف في بعض المناطق.
الجزائر تُقر عقوبة الإعدام لمفتعِلي حرائق الغابات. تشير التقديرات إلى أن أكثر من 200 شخص لقوا حتفهم في حرائق اندلعت في شمال شرق البلاد خلال فصل الصيف.

القوات الحكومية اليمنية تعلن استهداف مواقع "ذات قيمة عالية" في صنعاء بعد سماع دوي انفجارات قوية. القوات الحكومية اليمنية تشن غارات على صنعاء وصعدة وتعز، والتحالف الذي تقوده السعودية يعلن اعتراض مسيّرات وصواريخ حوثية، ويتهم جماعة أنصار الله بالهجوم على محطة طيبة للكهرباء في المدينة المنورة.

العال تلغي رحلاتها لإعادة إسرائيليين من دبي، ونتنياهو يقول إن مساعد طيار رحلة فلاي دبي "خضع لتلقين أفكار إسلامية متطرفة". رئيس الوزراء الإسرائيلي بنيامين نتنياهو يقول إن مساعد الطيار الذي حاول إسقاط طائرة ركاب كانت متجهة إلى إسرائيل "خضع لتلقين أفكار إسلامية متطرفة"، مشيراً إلى أنه سيتمكن في غضون أيام قليلة من تحديد ما إذا كان مساعد الطيار على صلة بإيران.

أزمة دبلوماسية بين إثيوبيا وإريتريا، وسط توتر متصاعد مع مصر. توترٌ إقليمي متصاعدٌ في القرن الأفريقي مع قطع إثيوبيا وإريتريا العلاقات الدبلوماسية، وتبادل طرد الدبلوماسيين مع مصر، وسط تجدد القتال في تيغراي.

"قوية وجميلة": لماذا نحن جميعاً بحاجة إلى دهون الجسم؟. لطالما نُظر إلى الدهون نظرة سلبية لسنوات عديدة؛ فثقافة الحمية الغذائية تحثنا على حرقها. ومؤخراً أبدى الخبراء قلقهم من عودة النزعة نحو النحافة المفرطة للظهور مجدداً.

"الاعتماد على الأمم المتحدة في هذا الظرف يضع العالم في مأزق كبير" - مقال في الغارديان. تسلط الصحافة البريطانية الضوء على تحولات كبرى تكشف "هشاشة" المنظومات الدولية والتقنية، بدءاً من المأزق الدبلوماسي العارم في أروقة الأمم المتحدة، وصولاً إلى أخلاقيات العقوبات القضائية ومخاطر العنصر البشري في الطيران.

ترامب يتوعّد إيران بـ"ضربة قوية جداً" إذا ثبت تورطها بحادثة طائرة "فلاي دبي". خلال دردشة مع صحافيين في البيت الأبيض، قال ترامب إنه يعتقد أن إيران متورطة في العملية، موضحاً "أقول إن الجواب هو نعم، استناداً إلى ما أسمعه، لكننا نعمل على هذا الأمر في هذه اللحظة بالذات".

Un nouveau bras de fer s’engage donc avec le régulateur.

RDC-France : de Kinshasa à Bunia, les enjeux de la visite de Jean-Noël Barrot. Le ministre français des Affaires étrangères se rend les 2 et 3 octobre en RDC, avant une conférence humanitaire à Paris. Il fera une étape, inédite pour le chef de la diplomatie française, dans l’est du pays.

Paiement instantané : Wave rallie la plateforme de la BCEAO et acte une nouvelle ère pour l’union monétaire. Avec sa plateforme de paiement instantanée, l’UEMOA entre dans l’ère du paiement interopérable entre banques et portefeuilles mobiles. Un bouleversement qui menace les revenus des opérateurs et redistribue les cartes.

États-Unis – Cameroun : Trump choisit l’artisan de ses accords d’expulsion comme ambassadeur à Yaoundé. Christian Jové Ehrhardt, responsable des très controversées expulsions de migrants vers des pays tiers, représente désormais Washington à Yaoundé. Une nomination qui éclaire les dessous de l’accord secret signé en décembre 2025 entre les États-Unis et le Cameroun.

Afrique du Sud, Algérie, Côte d’Ivoire, Égypte, Maroc : qui est prêt à jouer les plans B pour la CAN 2027 ?. Théoriquement, la Coupe d’Afrique des nations 2027 doit se tenir en Ouganda, en Tanzanie et au Kenya. Mais face aux retards qui s’accumulent, la CAF a commencé à sonder certains pays. En tête de liste : le Maroc, l’Algérie et l’Afrique du Sud.

Côte d’Ivoire, Burkina, Mali… Le boom des raffineries d’or face au scepticisme des géants miniers. L’Afrique de l’ouest multiplie les raffineries d’or pour transformer sa matière première sur place. Si obliger les artisans miniers à y envoyer leur or est une gageure, encourager les industriels à le faire est encore plus difficile. Analyse.

Au Sénégal, Petrosen espère lancer Sangomar 2 à l’horizon 2028. Ce 1er octobre, le directeur général de Petrosen, Thierno Seydou Ly, a annoncé vouloir entrer dans le deuxième phase de Sangomar d’ici à 2028. L’objectif serait d’ajouter 8 puits supplémentaires.

Les six jours les plus longs : comment s’est décidée la nomination de Fatima-Ezzahra El Mansouri à la primature marocaine. Le 23 septembre, le PAM arrive en tête des législatives. Mais passé les célébrations vient l’attente. Réserves religieuses, procès de personnalité, hypothèse Lekjaâ : récit des six jours durant lesquels une nomination qui semblait acquise a soudain cessé de l’être.

Aroni Chaudhuri (Coface) : « Le principal risque pour l’économie marocaine, c’est un risque social ». Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri prend les rênes d’un pays à l’économie solide mais qui éprouve des difficultés à réduire les inégalités. Aroni Chaudhuru, économiste chez Coface, passe en revue les défis qui attendent la nouvelle cheffe du gouvernement.

Les armées africaines, improbables recrues de la Force internationale censée stabiliser la bande de Gaza. Le plan de paix, encore théorique, du président américain, Donald Trump, prévoit que des troupes étrangères se déploient dans la zone contrôlée par le Hamas, et qu’elles étendent leur périmètre d’action au fur et à mesure que les islamistes déposent les armes et que l’armée israélienne se replie.

« En Afrique, il est encore temps d’éviter le modèle du tout-voiture ». En misant sur des projets technologiques calqués sur le modèle de mobilité des pays du Nord, les métropoles africaines aggravent leur étalement urbain au lieu d’y remédier, déplorent, dans une tribune au « Monde », les géographes Pape Sakho et Momar Diongue.

Mali : Amnesty International accuse l’armée et le Groupe Wagner de « crimes de guerre ». Les forces armées maliennes et les paramilitaires russes ont été plusieurs fois accusés d’avoir tué des civils lors d’opérations ces dernières années.

Au Maroc, l’attente anormalement longue de la nomination d’un nouveau premier ministre. Lors des deux précédentes élections législatives, le roi Mohammed VI a désigné le nouveau chef du gouvernement en moins de trois jours. Une semaine après la victoire du Parti Authenticité et modernité (PAM) aux législatives du 23 septembre, le silence du palais relance les interrogations sur la santé du monarque.

Au Maroc, le roi nomme pour la première fois une femme, Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri, à la tête du gouvernement. Près d’une semaine après la victoire du PAM, son parti, aux législatives, la maire de Marrakech a été désignée, mardi 29 septembre, première ministre du Maroc.

L’Ethiopie accuse l’Erythrée, le Soudan et l’Egypte de soutenir les rebelles. Le chef d’état-major général de l’armée éthiopienne a directement accusé, jeudi 24 septembre, les trois pays et « d’autres puissances extérieures » de soutenir la nouvelle alliance de groupes d’opposition qui mène depuis une semaine une offensive d’ampleur dans le nord du pays.

Quelques œuvres d’Hervé Yamguen. L’artiste camerounais présente ses dernières réalisations à la galerie Afikaris, à Paris. Au menu de l’exposition « Nos géographies intimes » : peintures, dessins, sculptures et masques. Jusqu’au 31 octobre.

Art contemporain d’Afrique : à Paris, Hervé Yamguen explore nos « géographies intimes ». L’artiste camerounais présente ses dernières œuvres dans la galerie Afikaris, située dans le 3ᵉ arrondissement de la capitale. Au menu de l’exposition, des peintures, dessins, sculptures et masques, reflets de ses vibrations intérieures. Jusqu’au 31 octobre.

Au Maroc, l’arrestation du maire de Tanger, suspecté de fraude électorale lors des législatives, plonge son parti, vainqueur du scrutin, dans la polémique. En poste depuis 2021, l’édile, membre du Parti authenticité et modernité, a été interpellé à Tanger, lundi 28 septembre, et placé en garde à vue. La justice le soupçonne d’avoir participé à une falsification massive de bulletins de vote.

L’Algérie, principal pays de départ de migrants vers l’Espagne. Depuis le début de l’année 2026, les Algériens sont la troisième nationalité la plus représentée parmi les entrées clandestines en Europe, après les Bangladais et les Soudanais.

L’Egypte hausse le ton face à l’Ethiopie sur le partage des eaux du Nil. Alors qu’Addis-Abeba s’enfonce à nouveau dans la guerre civile, Le Caire s’emploie à isoler diplomatiquement son voisin pour l’empêcher de contrôler unilatéralement le fleuve, dont l’Egypte dépend presque uniquement pour son approvisionnement.

Dans le nord du Nigeria, le nombre d’enlèvements augmente sous la pression de gangs criminels locaux et des djihadistes. Au moins 87 personnes ont été kidnappées samedi et dimanche dans les Etats de Zamfara et du Niger. Entre juillet 2025 et juin 2026, on dénombrait 7 825 victimes de prises d’otage, un chiffre en hausse qui fragilise le pouvoir, avant l’élection présidentielle de janvier 2027.

Au Maroc, malgré la nomination d’une première ministre, le plafond de verre demeure pour les femmes. Sur 395 députés élus au Parlement après le scrutin du 23 septembre, la représentation des femmes reste minoritaire (107) et cantonnée aux quotas. Toutefois, la nomination de Fatima Ezzahra El-Mansouri par le roi suscite l’espoir des associations féministes.

En Algérie, les députés étendent la peine de mort aux auteurs de feux de forêt. Le texte élargit également la peine capitale à de nouveaux cas d’enlèvements d’enfants accompagnés de violences graves, les autorités évoquant une recrudescence de ces actes ces dernières années.

Pourquoi l’Ethiopie replonge-t-elle dans la guerre ? Comprendre en trois minutes. Après plusieurs mois de tensions, les combats ont repris à la fin de septembre en Ethiopie entre l’armée fédérale éthiopienne et différents groupes rebelles, laissant planer la menace d’un nouveau conflit de grande ampleur. Une guerre civile avait déjà éclaté dans le pays entre 2020 et 2022.

En Egypte, l’arrestation de six journalistes d’un média d’investigation, signe de la nervosité du régime du président Al-Sissi. Ce coup de force sans précédent arrive au moment où les autorités doivent faire face à un contexte économique tendu et à des rivalités politiques qui s’aiguisent pour succéder au président Abdel Fattah Al-Sissi, au pouvoir depuis 2013.

Au Kenya, le lancement en un temps record du chantier de la raffinerie Dangote. Le magnat nigérian Aliko Dangote ambitionne de répliquer sa raffinerie de Lagos à Lamu, une région isolée face à l’océan Indien. Mercredi 30 septembre, en présence de chefs d’Etat africains, s’est tenue une cérémonie hautement politique et symbolique.

Pourquoi l’Algérie a élargi la peine de mort aux incendiaires et aux kidnappeurs d’enfants. Après les feux de forêts intenses et meurtriers de l’été, le chef de l’Etat, Abdelmadjid Tebboune, a souhaité élargir le nombre de « crimes capitaux », passibles de la peine de mort. Le pays respectait pourtant un moratoire sur cette question depuis 1993.

A Johannesburg, la découverte de onze corps révèle l’ampleur des violences à l’égard des femmes. Depuis juillet, des corps de femmes nues ou à moitié nues, violemment battues, ont été retrouvés en banlieue de Johannesburg. Si la thèse du prédateur en série s’amenuise, la réalité d’une extrême violence infligée aux Sud-Africaines au quotidien s’impose.

Guerre en Ethiopie : des attaques de drones ciblent la capitale, les forces gouvernementales gagnent du terrain dans le nord du pays. Après les frappes sur Addis-Abeba mercredi soir, le gouvernement éthiopien a décidé la fermeture de son ambassade à Asmara. En réponse, l’Erythrée a rompu tous ses liens diplomatiques avec l’Ethiopie.

Why Russia remains stubbornly insignificant to the Middle East Submitted by Joseph Massad on Thu, 10/01/2026 - 12:45 Moscow's call for Palestinian statehood is empty rhetoric from a state that chose Israel in 1948 and stands by it today through genocide in Gaza and war on Iran Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on 26 September 2026 (Charly Triballeau/AFP) Off In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly last week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov emphasised: "The time has also come to address the main issue in the Middle East - ensuring the Palestinian statehood on the basis of countless United Nations decisions." Support for Palestinian statehood has been Moscow's position since the Soviet Union backed partition in 1947, and it has remained so since the Russian Federation's establishment in December 1991. Rather than providing the Palestinians with substantial support against their Israeli colonisers, the Russian Federation has, since 1991, at best offered nothing more than empty diplomatic rhetoric in support of a defunct two-state solution while maintaining cordial relations with Israel . Even after Israel openly aligned itself with the all-out western war against Russia through the war in Ukraine, the Russians have not abandoned their alliance with Israel. In that alliance, and in its pretence of "both-sidesism" through continued support for the defunct two-state solution, the Russian Federation has fared much worse than the USSR. Aside from meaningless diplomatic declarations like Lavrov's last week, Russia's lukewarm support for Iran in the current war is hardly a major deviation from the Soviets' careful balancing act in the post-war period. The Soviet and subsequent Russian commitment to alienating the Arab public continues apace. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Far from forging a new path, the Russian Federation has refused to change its policies towards the Palestinians and Zionism, except by increasing trade and security coordination with Israel over the past three and a half decades. Its support for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which collaborates with Israel and the West, hardly counts as support for the Palestinians. Given these realities, it is curious that no one in Russia's ruling circles has thought of radically changing its failed Middle East policy. Soviet alternatives The Russian Bolsheviks, both Christians and Jews , had all along vehemently opposed not only Zionism but even the anti-Zionist Jewish nationalism of the General Jewish Labour Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia (known as the Bund), which called for non-territorial Jewish cultural autonomy. It was after the Russian Revolution and the establishment of the Soviet Union that Bolshevik opposition to Zionism became state policy, while their earlier opposition to Bundist Jewish nationalism wavered. The Bund soon dissolved itself , and most of its members joined the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU). Indeed, many former Bundists became officials in the party's Jewish Section (Yevsektsia), implementing Soviet cultural and linguistic (Yiddish) policies towards the union's Jewish population. It was after the Russian Revolution and the establishment of the Soviet Union that Bolshevik opposition to Zionism became state policy It was the Jewish Section of the CPSU that led the charge against Zionism in the country. Zionist organising became illegal in the USSR, and prominent Soviet Jewish and Christian figures railed against the settler-colonial movement in speeches and publications, describing Zionists as colonialists who aimed to subordinate indigenous Palestinian workers to British capital. At the same time, the Soviets embarked on a policy that continued the tsars' sponsorship of Jewish agricultural colonisation inside the country, which dated back to the late 18th century. Under the tsars, Russian Jews were dispatched to Siberia, southern Russia, the Caucasus and Crimea to establish agricultural settlements, a number of which were still prospering at the time of the Russian Revolution. The onslaught of the tsarist White armies and their western European sponsors against the revolution devastated the Pale of Settlement, where most Jews had lived under the tsars, killing upwards of 100,000 Jews and destroying the livelihoods of the survivors. It was in that context that the nascent Soviet government co-sponsored and co-financed a new project with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee to establish more agricultural colonies for Jews in southern Ukraine, the North Caucasus, the Volga region and Crimea. The project ran from 1924 until 1938, when the joint committee ran out of the funding to continue. Soviet Zion In 1934, the Soviets, who refused to create a "Jewish" province in Crimea because of opposition from the indigenous Crimean Tatars, created one in sparsely populated Birobidzhan . This was intended to satisfy anti-Zionist Jewish nationalists who saw the principled Soviet policies of fighting antisemitism and integrating Soviet Jews as the best riposte to settler-colonial Zionism. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); While many Jewish officials opposed the project, a pro-Birobidzhan article in the Communist International's (Comintern) International Press Correspondence (Inprecor) declared: Now proof has been furnished that the Jews, like all the other peoples, are able like pioneers, under the hardest physical conditions, to convert an undeveloped country into a country of socialist culture. There is no "Arab question", no conflict of imperialist interests, no flight from one anti-Semitism to another. That is the solution to the Jewish question by the Soviet Power. The article, by an author identified only as MZ, was titled "Socialist Construction in the Soviet Union: Biro Bijan, an Autonomous Jewish Province" and appeared in Inprecor, volume 14, number 32, on 1 June 1934. Indeed, it was the soft Zionist and hard anti-communist Hannah Arendt who admitted as much: "The Russian Revolution has dealt a blow to the first [Zionist] contention that the Jewish Question can be solved only in Palestine and that antisemitism is only to be eradicated by the building up of Palestine, in other words by the exodus of Jews from their former homelands." Still, the majority of Soviet Jews remained anti-nationalist and supported assimilation into Soviet society. Only a small percentage moved to Birobidzhan or to the agricultural colonies, while the majority moved to large Soviet cities in Russia, Belorussia and Ukraine, spurning Jewish nationalism in all its guises - Zionist, Bundist and Soviet-sponsored alike. By the Second World War, Jews were so integrated into Soviet society that more than 100 Jewish generals served during the war in the Red Army, which the Jewish Bolshevik Leon Trotsky had founded and led. The Soviets and their Communist International defended the Palestinians' right to revolt against the British and the Zionists in both the 1920s and the 1930s, condemning the Zionists outright. In the wake of the 1929 Palestinian Buraq Wall uprising, Georgy Safarov , deputy director of the Comintern's Eastern Department, strongly condemned the "Zionist colonies in Palestine", describing "the Jewish community in Palestine [as] a British imperialist avant-garde". By the end of the war and after the Holocaust, however, Stalin had made an about-face. Zionist reversal Zionist lobbying of Soviet embassies in Britain and Turkey helped, but was not the main reason. At the beginning of the Cold War, the reactionary Arab monarchies and the conservative Palestinian leadership were allied with the imperialist West. Their post-war alliances and hostility to communism did not endear them to the Soviets. Zionist pretensions to being committed socialists and non-partisan in the Cold War helped convince the Soviets to support a one-state solution for Palestinians and Jewish settlers or, failing that, the partition of Palestine into two states - one for the settlers and the other for the indigenous population. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); The Soviet ambassador to the UN, Andrei Gromyko, received new instructions from Moscow in April 1947 that upended the previous Soviet anti-Zionist position. Gromyko gave impassioned speeches in May and November 1947, defending the Jewish settlers' alleged right to establish a state in Palestine while blaming western European countries for failing to help Jews during the war. Zionism was built as a bulwark against socialism Read More » When Israel was proclaimed, the Soviets rushed to recognise it, earning the hostility of the majority of the Arab world and permanently alienating all Arab communist parties, which toed the Soviet line, from the Arab public. If the Soviets thought they had gained an ally in the Middle East by supporting the Zionists, they soon realised their miscalculation. Still, under Nikita Khrushchev, who had succeeded Stalin as party leader the previous year, the Soviet legation in Israel was upgraded to an embassy in June 1954. It was the Arab republics, however, that would prove the friendliest Arab regimes to the Soviets: Egypt from the mid-1950s, Iraq after 1958 and Algeria after 1962, followed by others. The Soviets continued their diplomatic relations with Israel, while their support for the Arab republics remained lukewarm compared with western imperialism's support for Israel and the reactionary Arab regimes. Israel's alliance with imperialism and hostility to the Soviets were such that it launched a campaign branding the Soviets, the first regime in the world committed to fighting antisemitism in word and deed, as "antisemites". As Jews in western countries refused to move to Israel and immigration dried up, the Israelis sought to bring Soviet Jews to populate their settler-colony. That was the context in which they charged the Soviets with antisemitism for refusing to allow Soviet Jews to leave for Israel. Diplomatic limits The Soviets cut off relations with the Jewish settler-colony after the Israeli invasion of three Arab countries in 1967. Israel then intensified its campaign against Soviet "antisemitism" until the Soviets finally succumbed and allowed large-scale Jewish emigration from 1971 onwards. Half of those who left chose the US rather than Israel. The relaxation was part of the Soviet attempt to maintain detente with the US, which led the anti-Soviet campaign on Israel's behalf. It was Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev who relaxed emigration restrictions between 1987 and 1989, allowing a million Soviet Jews to leave the collapsing USSR for Israel, the only country that would readily take them. Gorbachev re-established diplomatic relations with Israel in October 1991, and on 16 December that year, under US pressure, the Soviet Union voted to repeal the UN's "Zionism is racism" resolution, which the Soviets had supported in 1975. Unless it radically changes its Middle East strategy, Russia will remain an insignificant factor in the ongoing struggle to end Zionist settler-colonialism and Israeli regional imperialism If Stalin's about-face on Zionism was motivated by the Holocaust, the Cold War and the dearth of pro-Soviet Arab rulers, would the current western war against Russia, the genocide of the Palestinians and the anti-imperialism of Iran and the Lebanese and Palestinian resistance not be sufficient to prompt another reversal? It is true that all the Arab regimes, including the collaborationist PA, are in the West's back pocket today, as they were in 1948. They are not, however, the only players in the political field. Western support for the Zionist project was aimed, as the antisemitic Winston Churchill put it in his 1920 article "Zionism versus Bolshevism", at striking a blow against the Russian Revolution and "international communism", which he identified as a Jewish "world-wide conspiracy". Britain's Balfour Declaration , issued in 1917 in support of what Churchill called the "National Jews", five days before the triumph of the Russian Revolution, was engineered to prevent Russian Jewish support for the revolution. The plan failed. Under Gorbachev, however, the Soviet Union aptly cast one of its last votes at the UN to rehabilitate Zionism. By supporting the repeal of the "Zionism is racism" resolution days before the curtain dropped on the USSR, it erased the Soviet era's anti-Zionism once and for all. In view of this history, the Russian Federation should expect little change in its standing in the Middle East. Unless it radically changes its Middle East strategy, it will remain an insignificant factor in the ongoing struggle to end Zionist settler-colonialism and Israeli regional imperialism. But it is true to the extent that Labour’s desire for a reset was propelled by the party’s loss of support among voters angered by the Starmer government’s complicity in the Gaza genocide . That anger, shared by a large segment of the Labour party, had been made clear at the party’s conference last year when a motion , recognising the genocide and calling for action to end the UK complicity and a full arms embargo, was passed with overwhelming backing. Miliband asserts that the only path to peace and justice is via a two-state solution . But other solutions exist, including a single democratic state that respects the rights of all; it is for the Palestinian people, and not any external government, to decide which option prevails. Part of the reset being offered is a shift in the government’s response to the question of whether a genocide has been committed in Gaza. But what is missing is the crucial recognition that the ICJ has already invoked obligations on all states to act to prevent genocide. They mirror the recommendations laid out by a special UN commission, whose findings were formally accepted by Labour members last year. The map of the requirements was laid out in that 2025 conference motion - a ban on settlement goods which is now promised but must be fully enacted, including action against Israeli banks providing services to settlements; a full arms embargo including F35 components; and end to all trade that supports Israel's illegal actions. Today, the two countries maintain diplomatic relations only at the level of charge d’affaires. 'Foreign policy rarely decides elections in Brazil' Despite Lula’s stance on Israel over Gaza, three powerful caucuses operate at the parliamentary level. Known as the three Bs, they represent bullets, referring to legislators with a military background; beef, representing powerful agribusiness interests; and the Bible, representing evangelicals. Many evangelicals share the attachment to Israel that their co-religionists in the US hold, and wield similar political power as a voting bloc. Even as the executive branch under Lula tilted modestly against Israel, the legislature created the Brazil-Israel Parliamentary Front in November 2025, reviving a parliamentary vehicle documented as far back as 2004. Flavio Bolsonaro, one of its members, used its launch to signal that a government he led would restore close ties with Israel. “Even with a president who is more critical of Israel, the legislative base is becoming increasingly pro-Israel, largely because of the alliance between the evangelical caucus and the so-called ‘bullet caucus,’” said Santos. 'For most voters, the Israel-Palestine issue mainly reinforces existing loyalties, since the issue now follows Brazil's left–right divide' - Professor Feliciano de Sa Guimaraes In Brazil, the evangelical vote amounts to an estimated 40 million voters. Flavio Bolsonaro had 52 percent support among evangelical voters, against Lula’s 26 percent. In a second-round scenario, the figures were 62 percent and 32 percent respectively. “These religious groups have been the most fervent defenders of the State of Israel, or rather of an imagined Israel, conservative and deeply religious," said Magalhaes. “Foreign policy rarely decides elections in Brazil,” notes Feliciano de Sa Guimaraes, a professor at the Institute of International Relations at the University of Sao Paulo. “Jobs, living costs and public security matter far more to most voters. But international issues do affect presidential popularity,” said Guimaraes, who has been polling Brazilians on their stances on international relations, speaking to MEE. According to the latest Pew research earlier this year on international views of Israel, just over half of Brazilians had an unfavourable view of Israel, and more than 60 percent lacked confidence in Netanyahu. At the start of Israel’s war on Gaza, the “median Brazilian voter leaned pro-Israel”, Guimaraes noted. Since then, he said, it has been the “voter who moved closer to Lula, not the reverse”. “For most voters, the Israel-Palestine issue mainly reinforces existing loyalties, since the issue now follows Brazil's left–right divide,” said Guimaraes. ‘We must enter first’: Yemen’s female soldiers face war, danger and a changing society Submitted by MEE correspondent on Fri, 10/02/2026 - 09:14 Female officers say their role is especially important when searching women, protecting privacy and keeping communities safe A woman soldier walks through a market in Taiz city, Taiz governorate, Yemen, 21 September 2026 (Middle East Eye) Off Wearing her security uniform, usually without a Kalashnikov or even a sidearm, 36-year-old Tahani walks proudly through Taiz city's markets. While some locals remain uneasy about seeing women in military roles, others express pride and joy that Yemeni women are serving as soldiers. Female soldiers were largely absent from public view in Yemen before the war broke out in 2015. Today, women are serving across Yemen’s security apparatus, from police stations and prosecution offices to military checkpoints and other security posts. Tahani is one of thousands who joined the women's police force in 2022. Since then, she has served in various security offices, participating in search operations and home raids searching for criminals. "Yemen needs female soldiers just as it needs female teachers. When I heard about the recruitment for the women's police in Taiz, I told myself that the moment had come to achieve my dream," Tahani told Middle East Eye. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Tahani, from a poor rural area, was a housewife. After getting divorced, she struggled to support her only child, making this job a vital source of income. Every morning before heading to work, she cooks breakfast for herself and her son and prepares him for school. She then heads to the police station full of energy, ready to serve alongside her male and female colleagues. “There are women who visit the police station almost daily, and only I or one of my female colleagues can inspect them and assist officers with their cases,” Tahani added. Yemenis seek safety in Djibouti as African migrants continue arriving in Yemen Read More » “Yemeni society is conservative, and women usually prefer to deal with other women, so we do this job for the sake of Yemeni women.” One of Tahani’s key duties is participating in home raids. When a suspect is inside a home, or when police suspect one might be, she carries out the operation alongside other female and male officers. “This is one of the most dangerous tasks. We must be cautious and have our weapons drawn, and we never raid a home without a plan,” she said. “However, female soldiers must enter first because there are usually women inside, and our traditions do not allow men to enter a home where women are present.” Although she has the necessary tactical skills, Tahani said she has not yet had to fire at a suspect, as male soldiers typically cover her and her female colleagues from behind. Growing presence In 2014, there were 2,868 members of the women’s police force across the entire country. That number has grown over the past decade as both warring sides - the Houthis and the government - have recruited hundreds of female soldiers. Last year, the United Nations Development Programme helped build the capacity of 69 female officers and soldiers in the Aden Governorate, providing training to help them perform their duties professionally. With the recent escalation, almost all military and security units have intensified their efforts: inspections have doubled, and more raids targeting suspects have been carried out. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); “This is the most serious situation since I started my job in 2022, as there are more home raids requiring female soldiers to be present,” Tahani said. Yemenis turn to 'Ruqyah' faith healers as medical healthcare remains in crisis Read More » “My colleagues at checkpoints have also doubled their efforts, because, during war, weapons can be smuggled and sleeper cells can spread among residents, so we must stay vigilant.” Sali, 43, is a colleague of Tahani with more experience, having joined the women's police force in 2016 and served at checkpoints and police stations. She said that during military escalations, they double their efforts, and their duties extend beyond police stations into their daily lives and commutes. “Security awareness must be high in such situations. We have to monitor all activity and people around us to prevent crime before it occurs,” Sali told MEE. “Times of military escalation see a rise in sleeper cell activity, and many cells have already been apprehended. One of our key tasks is to monitor these threats and urge the community to remain cautious.” Sali added that they have also been raising awareness among residents not to post photos, videos, or text updates about sensitive security and military developments that could “serve the enemy in battle, such as the location of strikes or explosions”. Urgent need Captain Muamer Abdulmonem, a Yemeni army officer with more than 20 years' experience, told MEE that while female soldiers play a key role in routine security, their contribution becomes critical during military escalations. “During the recent escalation, there has been a dire need not only for female soldiers, but also for female volunteers. Many have been supporting the army and security forces, particularly by monitoring sleeper cells and unfamiliar individuals arriving in communities,” said Abdulmonem. He noted that some sleeper cells operate under the guise of displaced families, street vendors, or beggars, making surveillance a key responsibility for female security personnel. Conflict in Yemen transforms the lives of long-marginalised Muhamasheen minority Read More » “There is also an urgent need for female soldiers to search female travellers, as some have been exploited to smuggle contraband, including weapons. Men cannot search women in our society, so female officers must perform these inspections.” Although Yemen’s women’s police force was established in 2000, its presence remained minimal for years. Abdulmonem said that female soldiers have gained greater community acceptance and assumed a far more prominent role only over the last decade. Thaker, 31, the brother of Tahani, said the family initially hesitated to let her work as a soldier, but eventually accepted her role because she works alongside other women rather than alone. “Tahani works with women and deals with women, so she is like any other woman working in the civil sector, and the family has accepted that,” Thaker told MEE. “A respected woman can work anywhere to serve her country.” Thaker believes that women are entering all kinds of professions and that society must accept female soldiers, as it is society itself that needs them to interact with women. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Increasing acceptance Amni Qaheri, a resident who once dealt with the police when her phone was stolen, said she was happy to interact with female officers because it allowed her to speak and engage with greater freedom. “It was a good experience to see that there are female soldiers we can deal with. I hope their numbers increase, or even that a women’s police station is established where all the staff are women, so we can have an even higher level of freedom,” Qaheri told MEE. She is also searched by female soldiers whenever she enters Taiz city, and says she feels comfortable with the procedures because women are dealing with women and “they do their job perfectly”. Sociologist Hail Saeed said there is growing social acceptance of women working in the police force, though it remains uneven across different regions and demographics. Houthi missile and drone attacks kill dozens of Yemeni government troops Read More » “Some families and communities still harbour reservations due to the nature of security work, particularly regarding field operations or night shifts,” Saeed told MEE. He added that female soldiers play a vital role, especially in cases involving women and minors. “Having women in the police helps ensure greater privacy and comfort for female citizens during searches, interrogations, or when filing complaints,” Saeed said. “It also facilitates access to information that some women might hesitate to share with a male officer due to social customs in a conservative society.” Saeed believes community acceptance of female soldiers will continue to improve in the future, particularly if they engage effectively with the public. “Community acceptance may expand gradually if the work of female soldiers is linked to competence, discipline, and community service, while taking cultural and social sensitivities into account.” The names of female police officials have been changed on request. ‘Why the need for all this drama’: DG ISPR lampoons India's 'neutralised Pakistani terrorist' claims, presents him before media. Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry lampooned India’s claims of “neutralising” a “terrorist” allegedly linked to the Pakistani military, presenting the individual during a press conference on Thursday. The press briefing came after Indian media reported that an individual wanted in connection with the April 22 Pahalgam terrorist attack last year had been killed during an “encounter” in Indian Illegally Occupied Kashmir’s Korag area. Addressing the media, the DG ISPR said he would talk “about a so-called terrorist incident, a false flag that has been staged by the Indian political military”. He presented a five-point timeline, showing that the whole scenario began on Sept 29. “On the night of Sep 29, the Indian corps deployed in IIOK made a tweet, claiming that, based on joint intelligence reports, the Indian Army, police and CRPF launched an operation in general area of Korag, Yousmarg,” he read from a social media post by Chinar Corps. The DG ISPR then referred to another post by Chinar Corps on Sept 30 morning that claimed the Indian forces had found the body of a “Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist”. The military spokesperson noted that later, India’s ANI news outlet claimed that the deceased had been identified as Mohammad Asif, who had been inducted into the Special Services Group (SSG). The DG ISPR went on to say that India’s home affairs ministry and Press Information Bureau also reiterated the narrative. India’s home affairs ministry said the neutralisation of “Musa alias Asif Fauji” was part of an “ongoing long-sustained Operation Sheruwali” that was launched in May. “After six months of hard work, Musa alias Asif Fauji has been neutralised. Congratulations, applause,” Lt Gen Chaudhry retorted. He then read out India’s claims of Asif’s so-called involvement in various attacks: “Halan attack August 23, DKG attack December 23, Kandi attack May 2023, Shah Sitar attack May 2024, Shiv Khori attack June 2024, Gagangeer attack October 2024, Boota Pahari attack October 2024, and Basira attack April 2025.” The DG ISPR then noted that the Indian government also claimed to have neutralised three other “members of the group”. “After this [press conference], the shameful characters will have at least the shame to delete this,” he remarked. The DG ISPR also read out the Indian PIB’s narrative, which said their forces had killed “four senior LeT commanders”. He took a jibe at Indian media too for highlighting the claims: “Now they said, ‘Let’s jump in’. “So there comes News18 , Statesman , India Today , Hindustan Times , ABP Live , Indian Express ,” he said, as he displayed the screengrabs of these outlets’ reports on the matter. The DG ISPR then called Asif to join him during the presser, who said he was a resident of Attock district. “So here is that superman. You can see this superman. Please, come, my brother. Tell us about these achievements of yours, what all you have been doing,” Lt Gen Chaudhry quipped. ‘Here, alive and healthy’ Speaking before the media, Asif narrated: “Yesterday, some friends called me and told me there were reports on social media that I had been martyred by the Indian army in Kashmir. “To their concerns, I responded that I was here, alive and healthy.” Journalists at the ISPR press conference break into a laugh when Mohammad Asif, whom India claimed was killed in an oepration, appeared before them on Oct 1, 2026. — PTV News Asif said he also received calls from Indian numbers, asking him for his personal information, identity, whereabouts and his connection with the claims. “Through ANI on social media, I became aware of the reports that Indian media, using my personal data, had named me as a martyr in an operation in Kashmir,” Asif said. “I was surprised by whatever was happening as I was sitting in my home,” he remarked. Following the reports, Asif said that he informed his unit about the reports to clarify his position, and the unit asked him to block all the numbers calling from India and said that ISPR officials would contact him. Sharing details about himself, Asif said that he joined the Pakistan Army in the year 2000. “In 2005, I joined the SSG, performed my duty with courage for 18 years, and retired in 2023.” Asif added that he had also worked for a private security company for three years. “For the past three or four months, I have been living with my family in our home in Rawalpindi.” He termed the Indian allegations as “false, ignominious and disreputable”. “I condemn this. By the grace of God, I am alive and present before you.“ He further affirmed that he performed his duties with courage and that Pakistan responds face to face, not from behind. ‘Six reasons behind such dramas’ Five of the six “reasons” listed by ISPR DG Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry for what he said were India’s false flag operations. — screengrab via PTV News Taking on the mic, the DG ISPR maintained that there were “six reasons” behind “such dramas” by India against Pakistan. “It is a very shameful and embarrassing thing. No self-respecting nation does this.” ‘Cover own track of terrorism’ Explaining the first reason, Lt Gen Chaudhry said that India did those theatrics to “cover its own track of terrorism”. “So, there has to be some good reason,” he added. “India is the biggest sponsor of terrorism and a terrorist state in the world,“ the DG ISPR declared. “And its implication, involvement, direct and indirect terrorism in the region goes back decades,” he added. “Whether it’s Mukti Bahini or LTT, and now the TTP, BLA, and their funding, sponsorship and planning. It (India) has now become a victim of its own trait.” The military spokesperson highlighted that this terrorism was also “now taking on an internal dimension”. He elaborated: “They are not just terrorising the region or countries around the region; they are terrorising the Muslims inside India, and also the Kashmiris, Sikhs, Dalits, Christians, [residents of] Manipur, and tribals. “Some country which lives and breathes terrorism is at the same time very afraid that their dark face will be exposed, so they have to cover their tracks. What better way to cover their tracks than to start calling everyone else a terrorist?” Lt Gen Chaudhry then played a video clip on the “decades of lies that they have been feeding to their own people as well as to the world at large”. He accused India of jailing Muslim Kashmiris, adding: “They take them out, kill them, and stage that as a false flag operation, portraying it as a terrorist act.” The DG ISPR quipped: “This time they went ahead; they said this is not very spicy, let’s take an army soldier of Pakistan and portray him as one that we have killed.” He then brought attention to India’s involvement in transnational killings, saying, “This habit of false flag operations has further encouraged India to go for transnational killings.” He added, “Everyone whom they don’t like, they start calling terrorists, because they see their image.” The military spokesperson then played a video containing a clip of an Afghan minister saying “our DNA is one” as he referred to India. “That is the illegitimate child of this terrorism, which is on our western border,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said, referring to Afghanistan. “Because what better opportunity than to give this dirty work to someone who is ready to do it for certain coins and dollars and money,” he retorted. A soundbite by Afghan Agriculture Minister Mawlawi Attaullah Omari is played during a press conference held by Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry on Oct 1, 2026. — DawnNewsTV ‘Oppression in occupied Kashmir’ The DG ISPR then identified the second reason for the claims as the developments in occupied Jammu and Kashmir, describing it as the “biggest garrison of the world”. “What’s happening in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir plays a big role in the psyche and in the cognitive domain of these Indians,” he asserted. “For every 10th Kashmiri, there is an Indian soldier or a security person. There are nearly 1 million military, security, and intelligence CRPF and law enforcement there,” he pointed out, noting other acts such as arrests and demolition of houses. “And you cannot subside them; you cannot take out their desire to be counted. It’s a simple desire,” Lt Gen Chaudhry said, noting that Kashmiris wanted the right of self-determination as promised in a United Nations Security Council resolution. He stated that New Delhi had to stage such incidents to “portray that Kashmiris have no problem”, whereas the reality was otherwise due to the “oppression” being committed against them. “You have an internal problem, a great internal problem of oppression, of torture. [But] you don’t want to address it; you want to externalise it. You cannot externalise your internal issues. You cannot put this blame on Muhammad Asif.” ‘Obsession with Pakistan’ The third reason, the DG ISPR said, was India’s “obsession with Pakistan”. He remarked: “I think Pakistan, over a period of time, has got on their nerves so much that whatever happens, they want to put it on Pakistan. “And therefore, their politico-military leadership imagination and faculties have somehow been constrained and restricted. […] And that’s why we keep on requesting them very politely, asking them, please grow up.” The military spokesperson, as in May last year, urged India to come forward with evidence if it had any behind its claims and allegations. “If you are not ready to give proof to us, you can give it to any third party,” he offered. ‘Bollywood influence’ Lt Gen Chaudhry stated that the fourth reason was New Delhi being “very much influenced” by Bollywood, adding that “they have turned into encounter-istan from Hindustan”. “It is the story that is important; the facts are not important to Indians,” he said, declaring claims by India and its media as “fiction”. He quipped that for India, the “story should be clear, the story should be spicy”. “There should be action in it; it should be entertaining […] make the encounter look real, throw in a Pakistani — just an ordinary Pakistani won’t be fun, let’s put in a havaldar, let’s put in an SSG guard, then it will be thrilling.” ‘Shining India delusion’ Fifth reason, as per the DG ISPR, was a “delusional ‘Shining India’ complex” that the neighbour had. “They think that they are great,” he said, recalling the field marshal’s remarks that “they are great without greatness”. “They are historical without history, and the shine — this is the shine that you are seeing. It is not shine; it is shame,” he remarked, contending that India presumed it could “control the mind” of others in the world like it controls its media. ‘Politicisation of military’ At last, the military spokesperson explained that the “politicisation” of the Indian military was another reason behind such tactics. “We cannot comprehend that we would be able to come out with such a story and such claims which don’t exist,“ he said. He asserted that the Indian brigade, corps commander and army commander allowed this and took responsibility for it “because you are a political army now”. “Your [Indian Army] agenda is Hindutva-driven. Your agenda is pleasing your political masters.” Lt Gen Chaudhry added, “Unfortunately, we have to deal with such a wretched and low-life kind of enemy. It is unfortunate that we have such a neighbour who is an encounter specialist. “[…] This is what the world, Pakistan, particularly the region, and the world at large is facing.” India warned of ‘very harsh retribution’ Asked about whether the recent allegations could trigger another armed conflict between the neighbours, the DG ISPR affirmed that Pakistan’s armed forces were always ready for any such move and warned of a “very harsh” retribution. “As a consequence of this false flag, which has been exposed very early in its infancy, if they want to do anything, most welcome. “[…] But let it be clear, and we have clarified it before also, that this time we will not leave them so easily. This time the cost that Pakistan would inflict on their strategic folly will be very, very severe.” He reiterated, “If they think that they want to build this drama, any other drama, and on the basis of that they want to do it, they can try their luck.” He also disputed the impression that the international community had a lack of response to India’s transnational killings. While noting that the Foreign Office (FO) could give a more nuanced reply, he said, “I think the Indian facade is very well exposed to the whole world.” Lt Gen Chaudhry recalled that a US secretary of state, former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau , and Australian leaders were among those who had raised their concerns about such killings. Responding to another query, the DG ISPR said India was “unreliable” and a “country which believes in deceit, terrorism and which believes in having their own hegemony in the region”. “So, the only guarantee of peace against such a country is our own strength.” Asked about the current status of Indian spy Kulbhushan Jadhav , who was captured in Balochistan in March 2016, the military spokesman said the law ministry was the relevant forum to approach. “Whether he is alive or dead, it is smeared on India’s face and will remain so.” Responding to other questions, the DG ISPR also reaffirmed Pakistan’s right to self-defence against terror attacks emanating from Afghanistan, as well as declared that the counterterror fight “ cannot be sacrificed at the altar of anyone’s politics ”. Indian media’s claims Indian media had claimed that the supposedly slain individual was affiliated with the banned LeT and was a soldier of the Pakistan military. The claim, attributed to “sources”, named the individual as Mohammad Asif. It may be recalled that Indian media and authorities had made several allegations regarding Pakistani involvement in the April 2025 Pahalgam incident, but failed to substantiate them. “Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa was born on 07 March 1980. He joined the Pakistan Army in 2000 under service number PA-3106947 and retired with the rank of Havildar,” India’s ANI reported on Thursday. It also provided a detailed profile of Asif. “In 2005, Mohammad Asif was inducted into the Special Services Group (SSG). He served with 4 Commando ‘Yalgar’ Battalion and was posted to Balochistan from 2006 onward. During his deployment in Balochistan, he reportedly participated in approximately 10 operations against Baloch insurgents and is credited with 13 personal kills,” the ANI news report stated, adding that Asif was also part of the security detail of former president Pervez Musharraf. It was stated by ANI that Asif was “wanted in the Pahalgam terror attack”, and the claim was repeated by the Indian Army’s Chinar Corps — part of the Northern Command and headquartered in occupied Kashmir. The corps primary area of responsibility is the Kashmir area of operations. In May 2025, a four-day conflict between Pakistan and India was sparked by an attack on tourists in occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam, which New Delhi, without evidence, linked to Pakistan. Islamabad had strongly denied responsibility while calling for a neutral investigation . After New Delhi launched deadly air strikes in Punjab and Azad Kashmir on May 7, Pakistan said it downed at least six Indian aircraft in air-to-air combat, later raising the tally to eight . After tit-for-tat strikes on each other’s airbases, it took American intervention on May 10 for both sides to finally reach a ceasefire . During that conflict, Indian media had been heavily criticised for beating the war drums and regurgitating fake news fed by Indian government sources. Many mainstream Indian channels had also aired inflammatory anti-Pakistan and anti-Muslim content. India’s ranking in the Reporters Without Borders’ World Press Freedom Index has deteriorated sharply over the past decade. The country ranked 122nd in 2010 but fell to 157th out of 180 countries in 2026. In April, on the first anniversary of the Pahalgam attack, Pakistan had rejected a renewed Indian propaganda campaign linking it to the attack, deploring that the neighbouring country was focusing on “weaponising its false narrative” in the midst of a regional crisis sparked by the US-Israel war on Iran.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs390.66 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs399.34 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable for Oct 2 (Friday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Sept 29 appreciated the success of the scheme , saying that it reflected a “whole of government” approach. Chairing a meeting of the National Steering Committee on Fuel Subsidy to review the implementation of the scheme, the deputy premier noted that the information, IT and petroleum ministries, as well as the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra), the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and all provinces, had made “concerted” efforts for the scheme. It was noted that to date, around 7.60 million registrations have been successfully made, and the token redemption process has entered the second week. Moreover, 7.71m tokens have been redeemed. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

PM Shehbaz met Trump at reception banquet on UNGA sidelines. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met United States President Donald Trump during the reception banquet hosted by the latter in honour of world leaders, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York last month, according to details released by the Press Information Department (PID) on Thursday. The PID shared photographs, released by the White House, of the two leaders standing together, smiling and shaking hands. No further details about the interaction were provided. The UNGA debate ran from Sept 22 to 26, with a final sitting on Sept 28. PM Shehbaz addressed the session on Sept 25 and was also mentioned by US President Donald Trump in his speech, who called him a “terrific man”. The premier also held bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the UNGA with world leaders, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. The premier’s official visit to New York, him meeting Trump and his participation in the UNGA debate came as Pakistan plays the role of a mediator for de-escalation between the US and Iran. Earlier this year, PM Shehbaz and Trump were also together at the signing of the charter for the “ Board of Peace ” — which has been constituted primarily to provide a roadmap to end the Israeli assault in Gaza — in January. Then, they also met at the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace in Washington, DC in February. State-run APP reported that an informal meeting was held between the two at the end of the summit. During the interaction, the two leaders expressed mutual goodwill and shook hands, the APP report said, adding that the US president also embraced PM Shehbaz. The premier had also met with Trump, alongside other world leaders, at a ceremony following the signing of a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas at the Sharm el-Sheikh Peace Summit in Egypt in October 2025. The two leaders had met for the first time at the Oval Office in Washington on September 25, 2025 in which they discussed regional security and cooperation among other matters. This was also around a UNGA session. The premier was accompanied by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, while the US president was joined by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The two sides had discussed regional security and cooperation along the lines of counter-terrorism, among other matters.

Violence-linked deaths surge 83pc. • Balochistan accounts for nearly 59pc of total fatalities in third quarter of 2026 • CRSS records 1,415 deaths, 558 injuries across 385 incidents • TTP becomes deadliest group, inflicting 117 deaths ISLAMABAD: Pakistan recor­ded a sharp 83 per cent increase in violence-linked fatalities during the third quarter of 2026, re­­versing a declining trend reported in the first and second quarters as terrorism and counter-terrorism deaths surged nationwide. The escalation, according to a report by the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), was largely driven by Balochistan, where fatalities more than tripled and the province accounted for nea­­rly 88pc of the national increase. The southwestern province overtook Khyber Pakhtunkhwa as the country’s worst-hit region in both violence-related deaths and recorded incidents. The CRSS report recorded at least 1,415 violence-linked fatalities and 558 injuries among civilians, security personnel and outlaws during Q3 2026, across 385 incidents involving terrorist attacks and counter-terrorism operations. Balochistan and KP remained the epicentres of violence, jointly accounting for 98pc of all fatalities during the period. Balochistan recorded 829 deaths, nearly 59pc of the national total, while KP reported 556 fatalities, accounting for more than 39pc. Balochistan also witnessed the highest number of violent incidents, with 186 cases, representing more than 48pc of all incidents recorded in the quarter. KP followed closely with 173 incidents, or nearly 45pc of the total. However, KP suffered the highest number of injuries, with 376 cases, while Balochistan recorded 163 injuries. The report said the surge from Q2 to Q3 marked the highest escalation in violence since 2021, ending the declining quarter-on-qua­rter trend observed during the first and second quarters of 2026. The increase was primarily lin­ked to Balochistan, where fatalities jumped 213pc compared with the previous quarter, rising from 265 deaths in Q2 to 829 in Q3. KP also recorded a rise in violence, with fatalities increasing by more than 17pc, from 475 to 556. Outlaws accounted for the majority of deaths, with 921 fatalities, or more than 65pc of the total, following nearly 154 security operations. Their deaths more than doubled, increasing by 103pc from 453 in Q2 to 921 in Q3. However, the rise was not limited to militant fatalities. Civilian deaths increased by nearly 36pc, from 187 to 254, while security personnel fatalities rose by more than 79pc, from 134 to 240. Combined civilian and security personnel deaths climbed by nearly 54pc, reaching 494. Among groups claiming resp­o­nsibility for attacks, the TTP emerged as the deadliest in Q3 2026, with 13 claimed attacks causing 117 deaths and 65 injuries. The BLA claimed five attacks that killed 34 people and injured 42, while HGB-IUM claimed three attacks that caused 27 fatalities and 129 injuries, the highest injury toll among the listed groups. Published in Dawn, October 2nd, 2026

Islamabad hints at cautious shift on US sanctions against Iran. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan on Thursday signalled a cautious shift in its approach to the newly imposed US sanctions on Iran, saying it would adhere to “all applicable sanctions regimes” under international and domestic law, a formulation that goes beyond Islamabad’s earlier emphasis on international law and bilateral trade commitments with Tehran. “Pakistan is a responsible member of the international community and adheres, and shall continue to adhere, to all applicable sanctions regimes in accordance with international and domestic laws,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing. The spokesperson did not explain what Islamabad considers “applicable” even though there is a fine difference between restrictions being legally applicable or practically applicable. The shift is nevertheless significant because when the US announced its latest sanctions against Iran, the then FO spokesperson Tahir Andrabi had said: “About trade with Iran, Pakistan is following international law and our bilateral trade agreements with Iran.” FO reiterates commitment to strategic ties with Washington, rules-based international system Technically, the earlier formulation placed the emphasis on Pakistan’s international legal obligations and its bilateral commitments to Iran while the new one is broader, bringing “all applicable sanctions regimes” and “domestic law” into the framework. That does not mean US unilateral sanctions automatically become binding international law for Pakistan, but it’s an acknowledgement that their practical reach can extend to Pakistani banks and companies because they operate within the international financial system and depend on access to dollar clearing, correspondent banking and financial messaging networks. SWIFT, the international financial network, neither works as a sanctions authority nor does it decide whether transactions are lawful, but it says responsibility for compliance rests with the financial institutions handling transactions and the relevant national and international authorities. SWIFT, which is incorporated under Belgian law, has previously disconnected Iranian banks to comply with European sanctions. This showed how sanctions adopted by a jurisdiction to which SWIFT is legally subject can affect a bank’s access to the international financial messaging network. For Pakistan, the issue is therefore less about complying with US sanctions and more about the financial consequences of dealing with Iranian entities because US secondary sanctions can expose foreign financial institutions to restrictions on their access to the US financial system, including correspondent or payable through acc­ounts. Washington has specifically warned of such exposure as part of its expanded Iran sanctions campaign. Therefore, the new Foreign Office formulation appears to leave Islamabad room to take those risks into account without explicitly accepting the US unilateral sanction as legally binding. Here the assertion about compliance with domestic laws comes into play as this potentially gives Islamabad regulatory space to restrict or limit Iran-related transactions on the basis of Pakistani banking, foreign exchange and AML requirements. For instance, State Bank’s Pakistan-Iran trade mechanism expressly requires clarity that transactions with Iran do not involve entities subject to international sanctions. Due to this clause, the businesses have been generally cautious about transacting with Iran, even before the latest sanctions. However, the government has per se not announced a suspension of trade with Iran or any decision to join the US sanctions campaign. The Foreign Office spokesman also sought to underline Pakistan’s relationship with Washington. “Pakistan highly values its enduring and multifaceted strategic partnership with the United States and remains fully committed to further strengthening its long-standing diplomatic, economic and security ties with Washington,” Mr Khan said. At the same time, Islamabad reaffirmed its commitment to multilateralism and international law. “Pakistan reaffirms its commitment to a rule-based international system rooted in multilateralism and international law,” Mr Khan said, adding that Islamabad remained in “constant and constructive communication with all relevant stakeholders”. The balancing act comes at a time when Pakistan is trying to preserve its role as an intermediary between the US and Iran. Mr Khan said Pakistan would continue urging US and Iran to exercise restraint and settle their differences through diplomacy. “Pakistan, being a mediator in communication between Iran and the United States, believes that it is important to continue urging both sides to exercise restraint, resolve outstanding issues through dialogue and diplomacy, and honour their respective commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding ,” he said. Pakistan believes this remains the “only viable pathway” to resolving the conflict peacefully, he added. Published in Dawn, October 2nd, 2026

IMF praises oil crisis handling, urges gas sector reforms. • Seeks faster work on targeted gas subsidies, Rs3.6tr circular debt • Acknowledges power sector’s improvement in recoveries, loss reduction • Govt, lender to discuss direct cash support for deserving power consumers next week ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has appreciated Pakistan’s handling of the oil crisis without supply disruptions or an additional budgetary burden despite regional challenges during six months of the US-Iran conflict , but it asked the authorities to expedite groundwork for managing the rising gas sector circular debt and providing targeted subsidies to consumers below the poverty line. Informed sources told Dawn that initial discussions on a proposed plan to shift gas-sector subsidies from consumer tariffs to BISP-based direct transfers had concluded that the “gas sector is far from ready given data and ownership-related challenges”. As a result, the application of a uniform tariff linked to the average prescribed gas price of around Rs1,700 per million British thermal units (mmBtu), worked out by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra), appeared premature. The Petroleum Division, led by Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, has been advocating uniform gas rates, as advised by Ogra, to cover the actual cost of supply, which is around Rs1,700-1,750 per mmBtu for the two gas utilities, reduce cross-subsidies from the industrial sector and curtail gas-sector debt. The debt has now risen to around Rs3.6 trillion, including principal payables of about Rs1.8tr and an almost equivalent amount in accrued interest and late payment surcharges. Another Petroleum Division proposal to increase the petroleum levy by a couple of rupees to finance part of the gas-sector circular debt has not found favour at relevant government forums and therefore has not been taken up with the IMF. The introduction of a protected category for domestic consumers, involving gas prices of Rs200-350 per mmBtu, had widened the pricing gap and resultantly added to circular debt, the division suggested. Only four of the 12 consumer slabs covered the cost of gas supply during winter, while rates remained below breakeven levels for around eight months of the year even after the imposition of substantial fixed charges. Sources said discussions with the visiting IMF staff mission showed that documentation of gas-meter ownership and premises remained a serious problem in a large number of cases. Consumers often avoid reporting changes in names or property ownership for decades to avoid fresh security charges and other formalities, making it difficult to identify households below the poverty line on the basis of meter data. The problem was even more prono­unced in the commercial sector, where titles often remained unchanged while premises changed hands on “pagri”. In contrast, documentation in the power sector was considerably more advanced despite its substantially larger consumer base. Therefore, the IMF staff is not yet convinced by the workability of the groundwork done so far, although the Fund has consistently been insisting on targeted gas subsidies and has advised further deliberations with consultants to develop a more workable mechanism over the longer term. The Fund also acknowledged Pakistan’s management of petroleum prices without creating an additional burden on the budget or facing product shortages. Sources said it noted that some other regional countries had faced supply shortages, additional burdens on national budgets or state-owned corporations, or both higher fiscal costs and supply disruptions. The IMF had initially raised questions over an increase of Rs65-70bn in power-sector circular debt, which stood at Rs1.675tr at the end of June 2026. However, it recognised that the power sector had actually “overperformed” on efficiency targets, including bill recoveries and loss reduction, while the overall increase in debt was caused by around Rs95bn in lower disbursements by the Ministry of Finance on account of tariff differential subsidy, based on the ministry’s own subsidy calculations. The Ministry of Finance also endorsed these figures but reported that the budgeted subsidy was higher than the actual requirement calculated on the basis of units supplied. It was also noted that power-sector circular debt could have declined further had K-Electric paid around Rs200bn on time instead of holding up disbursement through litigation. It was reported that the high court and appellate tribunal had upheld Nepra’s decision envisaging around Rs200bn in savings to power companies, although KE could still pursue further legal remedies.
