Trump calls Iran’s Hormuz offer ‘not enough’. • US president warns strikes against Tehran could resume after midterms; Washington sanctions Iran’s top carmakers, rail operators • Pezeshkian says his country is open to dialogue; Putin hopes the strait reopens, says Russia’s offer to take enriched uranium still stands PRESIDENT Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as “simply not enough”, warning that military action against Tehran could resume after the midterm elections and predicting long-term peace with the country is unlikely. In an interview with Time Magazine , Trump said he had seen “some aspects” of the Iranian proposal regarding the strait, but deemed it “simply not enough”. Asked why he rejected the proposal, Trump said: “Because things that I wouldn’t have ap­­proved a year ago I wouldn’t have today.” Regarding Tehran’s past threats to close the waterway, Trump said: “There was always a threat they had, and it worked for a little while. But we basically closed it on them. You know, they said we’re going to close. I said, ‘Well, if you close it, you’re going to have big trouble.’ We took it over.” In response to his previous UN remarks about annihilating Iran, Trump told Time, “Yeah, I would do that. It’s possible.” Defending his title as the “president of peace”, he argued, “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world. With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.” He noted post-midterm bombings remain possible, adding, “We have a lot of weapons.” Addressing a Pentagon report citing munitions shortfalls caused by Operation Epic Fury in Iran, Trump dismissed it as “mostly fake news”. Acknowledging some ammunition forms are lower, he said the US is “stocking up at levels we’ve never done before”. Separately, Trump claimed on Truth Social that while eliminating a nuclear threat typically takes four to six weeks, he “did it in one night”, adding that the remainder of the seven-month conflict ensures it stays that way. He told Time the US destroyed Iran’s navy, air force and radar systems. Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Thursday that Tehran would defend itself but remains open to dialogue, as the country weighs a US response to its proposal to resurrect a collapsed mid-June ceasefire, IRNA news agency reported. “We defend the rights of our society with dignity and pride, and we have never run away from dialogue and will not do so, although the United States has targeted our country three times despite having signed the agreement,” Pezeshkian told entrepreneurs, according to the official IRNA news agency. Iran accused the US of violating the agreement by maintaining a naval blockade. “The US should get the idea of bringing us to our knees with terror and martyrdom out of its head,” Pezeshkian said. He added Iran is seeking to expand import-export avenues via land with Pakistan, Iraq, Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan, despite “restrictions at sea”. To counter those alternative trade routes, the US Treasury Department imposed fresh sanctions on Thursday on Iran’s rail and automotive conglomerates. The measures target Iran Khodro Company and SAIPA, which represent more than 90pc of Iran’s domestic auto market, alongside the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company and top private freight lines. The sanctions fall under “Operation Ec­­o­­­nomic Outcast” , launched on Aug 24, to cut Tehran’s funding for warfare and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the action “directly targets Iran’s enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime’s revenue once and for all”. Separately, Russian President Vladimir Putin told a forum he hoped the Strait of Hormuz would be open to shipping and that sanctions on Iran would eventually be lifted, noting Russia’s proposal to receive enriched uranium from Iran remained on the table. UAE probes possible terror link in flydubai incident. DUBAI: The United Arab Emirates announced on Thursday it is investigating a possible terrorist link to an apparent attempt by a co-pilot to crash a flydubai passenger jet headed to Israel. The dramatic events on Wednesday ended with the plane making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia and passengers receiving a hero’s welcome from Israeli Prime Minis­ter Benjamin Netanyahu upon arriving in Tel Aviv. Disaster was averted on flight FZ1073 from Dubai after the wounded captain unlocked the cockpit door, allowing passengers to subdue the attacker. Passengers described ru­­shing the cockpit after the flight suddenly nosedived, losing nearly 14,000 feet of altitude in less than 30 seconds over Saudi Arabia. Israel says initial assessment points to co-pilot acting alone; mental health concerns not ruled out The airline stated that an off-duty Dubai Reserve crew member travelling on the flight diverted and safely landed the aircraft in Tabuk. Both pilots were hospitalised after sustaining injuries. The UAE’s chief prosecutor said an investigation has been launched to dete­rmine circumstances and motives, including whe­th­­er the incident was linked to terrorist activity or inv­olved prior planning. UAE judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft flies under its flag. Flydubai suspended flig­­hts to Israel during the inv­estigation and warned aga­inst premature speculation. Two Israeli security officials said on Thursday that Israel’s initial assessment is that the co-pilot, identified by an Israeli official as an Omani national, likely acted alone. Israel’s envoy to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, cautioned that no motive had been determined. Netanyahu called the event a serious security incident, but told CBS News that mental health could not be ruled out. “He’ll be, I assume, moved very quickly to Dubai,” Netanyahu spoke of the alleged attacker, who was being questioned in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hailed the captain, Indian national Smit Ma­chchhar, for his “extraordinary bravery”. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was hospitalised. Passengers were also lauded for preventing a mid-air catastrophe. Yaniv Hayun, one of the men who incapacitated the attacker, described running to the cockpit as the plane plummeted. “We pulled the assailant out; I pulled him out. After I pulled him out, we took control of the plane, I pul­led up the yoke, and I str­aightened the plane out a bit,” Hayun told reporters. Hegseth says US slashed 20pc of its military leadership cadre. • Describes cuts as ‘accountability’, while critics call them a purge • Musk set to co-lead Pentagon Project Meridian, a study on future of warfare WASHINGTON: Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that the United States has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20 per cent, in a move he said is aimed at “accountability”. Hegseth suggested the cuts targeted officers who failed to get on board with his efforts to ensure the military is focused on war-fighting rather than the “woke” policies of previous administrations, describing the reductions as an “accomplishment”. “The number-crunchers say we fired 10pc of the generals and admirals across the force,” Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base, saying: “We’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10pc.” “So yes, 20pc reduction across the board,” he said. “The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue.” The address to junior officers and enlisted personnel at Quantico came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focu­sed on leftist “woke” ideas, and in need of major shake-up. He said on Wednesday that top officers who “responded positively” to the previous spe­e­ch are “leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations”, while th­­ose who did not “no longer work here”. “We are no longer the woke department or the we­ak department,” Hegseth said. “Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors — just tough, ready, committed troops.” Hegseth ordered major cuts to the US military — including a 10pc reduction to the overall number of generals and admirals, and a 20pc decrease in the highest four-star ranks — in May 2025. Musk’s return Meanwhile, tech billionaire Elon Musk will make a return to officially advising US President Donald Trump’s government by co-leading what the Pentagon called a study on the future of war. Musk served as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), where he spearheaded sweeping job cuts across the US federal government, before departing in May 2025. In a speech at the Quantico military base, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth said “Project Meridian” will be “an effort led by America’s best minds to study the future of warfare”. “We are leveraging a unique source of American advantage, one our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists,” Hegseth said. Musk will be a co-leader of Project Meridian alongside Palmer Luckey, the 34-year-old co-founder of defence technology company Anduril Industries, and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year-old Republican former House speaker. Musk’s companies are already major Pentagon contractors, including SpaceX building satellite networks for Trump’s planned “Golden Dome” missile defence shield. On Tuesday he was seated next to Trump at a lunch with artificial intelligence executives, where he joined other tech leaders in signing a voluntary AI safety accord that the president described as “morally binding”. Last week, Musk attended the state dinner Trump hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, and in May he flew to Beijing on Air Force One as part of the business delegation accompanying Trump on his state visit to China. 'Grave provocation': Pakistan condemns Houthi attack on power facility in Madina. Pakistan on Friday strongly condemned an attack by the Houthi militia on the Taibah power distribution station in Madina on Sept 29, describing it as a “grave provocation” and a threat to regional peace and security. In a statement, the Foreign Office (FO) said the attack targeted civilian infrastructure supplying electricity to the Holy Prophet’s (PBUH) Mosque. “The sanctity of the Two Holy Mosques and the safety of worshippers and pilgrims must be respected under all circumstances,” the FO said. It called for an “immediate and unconditional” end to what it described as “reckless actions”, saying such attacks also constituted a grave threat to regional peace and security. The FO reaffirmed Pakistan’s “unwavering solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and expressed full support for the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security. “Pakistan stands firmly with Saudi Arabia in its efforts to safeguard the Two Holy Mosques, protect its people and ensure the safety of pilgrims,” the statement said. The FO added that Pakistan had been and would continue to make efforts to achieve lasting peace and stability in the region. The statement comes as Yemen’s Saudi-led coalition accused the group of striking an electricity distribution station in Madina, which provided power to the Prophet’s (PBUH) Mosque. However, the Houthis have denied the accusation. The attack came as fighting intensifies in Yemen, where government forces said they carried out attacks on the militia’s targets. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said a drone struck the Taibah electricity distribution station at 5:11 am (07:11am PKT) on September 29. “The investigation and evidence gathered by the competent authorities have confirmed the involvement of the terrorist Houthi militia in planning and executing this cowardly terrorist act, based on after-action review and the wreckage of the drone used,” he said in a statement. The coalition said one transformer was taken out of service without affecting the wider electricity network. Saudi Arabia said earlier in September that it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Makkah before it entered restricted airspace over the city. The coalition described that incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Makkah since 2017, while the Houthis denied targeting Makkah or any other Islamic holy site. The latest escalation is the most serious fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis since a UN-brokered truce largely halted cross-border attacks in 2022. Hostilities resumed this year after the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in July and began attacking Saudi territory and shipping, while Houthi forces also made major territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes in Yemen and backed government forces fighting to push back the Houthis. Against this backdrop, Pakistan, which has signed two defence agreements with Riyadh, has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. The first one, the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA), was signed in Sept 2025, under which the two countries pledged that any attack on either nation would be treated as an act of aggression against both. The two countries are also parties to the Makkah Defence Alliance, which also includes Turkiye. The pact was signed on August 7 and provides that an attack on one member state would be treated as an attack on all. The military leadership of the three countries also held a meeting in Riyadh last month. During the meeting, the military leaders expressed a shared determination to “immediately translate” their commitments under the Makkah Defence Alliance into effective military cooperation. On September 30, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that Pakistan was “there to help” Saudi Arabia in any conflict. ‘Provocative attacks’ The incident has drawn harsh criticism from Muslim countries. Turkiye strongly condemned the alleged attack and voiced support for Saudi Arabia. “We strongly condemn the Houthis’ attack on civilian infrastructure” in Madina, the foreign ministry said. “These provocative attacks, which threaten Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and security and target the sacred values of the Islamic world, must cease immediately and unconditionally.” Turkiye said it reiterated its “strong support for Saudi Arabia” and called for steps to prevent further escalation. Qatar also condemned the attack. In a statement, Doha said it was “a grave assault on the sanctity of Islamic holy sites”, a violation of Saudi sovereignty and international law. It reaffirmed its “full solidarity” with Riyadh and said the kingdom’s security was an integral part of Gulf security. The League of Arab States joined the chorus, calling the attack “an unacceptable transgression”. The organisation said the attack “provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide” and represented a dangerous escalation. Al-Azhar, the Cairo-based institute of Sunni Islamic learning, also denounced the incident. It said, “Targeting Madina provokes the sentiments of Muslims worldwide”.

India's Cockroach Janata Party, student groups to protest, demand poll chief's resignation. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will face renewed pressure on Friday as the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janata Party and a separate coalition of student and activist groups stage fresh protests, demanding the resignation of the elections commission chief over a controversial voter roll revision. The CJP will rally in Mumbai and plans to expand demonstrations nationwide in the coming days, while student and civil society groups will gather at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. The protests mark the latest escalation in a dispute that has put unprecedented scrutiny on India’s Election Commission, long regarded as one of the country’s most trusted institutions. The protesters’ main allegation is that the commission manipulated voter rolls in ways that favour Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The commission and the government have denied the allegations. Pressure on Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar intensified last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported the election chief’s two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times over the past 10 months over voter-list revisions, registration procedures and the commission’s digital systems. The Election Commission has said differing views are a normal part of internal deliberations and that all its actions were lawful. “We have been asking and demanding for a change but nothing of that is going to happen, if our only tool that is left to change anything in our society ‘the right to vote’ is taken away from us,” Saurav Das, CJP’s convenor, told Indian news agency ANI on Thursday. “We will only end the protest after Gyanesh Kumar resigns.” The controversy centres on a nationwide voter-verification exercise launched last year that critics say has led to millions of eligible voters being removed from electoral rolls. The commission says the exercise is intended to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible voters and ensure the accuracy of electoral rolls. Opposition parties led by the Congress party are also set to begin protests demanding Kumar’s resignation on October 6. The CJP, a youth movement that emerged earlier this year from online frustration over unemployment and leaked examination papers, has become an unexpected political force. Led by Abhijeet Dipke, the party gained national prominence after spearheading mass protests over exam-paper leaks that led to the resignation of India’s education minister, one of Modi’s most significant political setbacks in recent years.

Arab-Israeli politician withdraws from October election after Supreme Court signals disqualification. Arab Israeli politician Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy on Thursday from October’s parliamentary election after Israel’s Supreme Court indicated a majority of its judges supported barring him from the race. Arab Israeli parties are seen by political analysts as potential kingmakers in the October 27 election , with polls showing neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s coalition nor the main opposition bloc on course for a majority. Abu Shehadeh leads the left-wing Palestinian Balad party and served in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, from 2019 to 2022. The Balad leader was withdrawing his candidacy, but the decision did not mark the end of his political struggle, his party said in a statement, adding that he would remain the party’s leader. Last week, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify Abu Shehadeh at the request of far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir. The move came after an article in which Abu Shehadeh described Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack as an “important historical event”. He has denied supporting the attack, but the remarks drew sharp criticism. The Supreme Court convened on Thursday to hear Abu Shehadeh’s appeal against the disqualification. Rather than issue a ruling, the court proposed that he voluntarily withdraw after signalling that most of its judges favoured excluding him from the election. It gave him until Friday morning to decide. Abu Shehadeh had little choice but to withdraw in order to avoid a formal disqualification that would have “grave consequences for the country’s political and parliamentary life”, Balad said. ‘Severe blow’ Disqualifying candidates is rare in Israel, where the Supreme Court has historically overturned most bans approved by the elections committee. Under Israeli law, candidates can be barred only if they deny Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state or support armed struggle by an enemy state or a terrorist organisation against Israel. Adalah, the Israeli rights group representing Abu Shehadeh, accused the Supreme Court of effectively disqualifying him by pressuring him to withdraw. “A Palestinian leader has been forced out of the Israeli Knesset elections after the Supreme Court made clear it would remove him,” the group said in a statement to AFP . Adalah said Abu Shehadeh’s decades of public life as a human rights activist, legislator and party leader demonstrated his “consistent and unequivocal opposition to violence of any kind”. “It is a severe blow to the right of Palestinian citizens to be represented and to stand for election.” Besides Abu Shehadeh, the elections committee last week barred two Arab electoral lists: the United Arab List and the Joint List, a three-party alliance that includes Balad. The Supreme Court is due to continue hearing appeals from those parties on Friday. Arab Israelis account for about 20 per cent of the country’s population. Most identify as Palestinians. They are descendants of Palestinians who remained within Israel’s borders after the state’s creation in 1948 and have long complained of discrimination compared with Israel’s Jewish majority.

New islands appear after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupts. Two new islands have emerged in waters surrounding Mount Anak Krakatau following a major eruption last month that grounded flights for days, the head of Indonesia’s volcano monitoring agency said Friday. The islands were spotted in satellite images of the water-filled caldera in which Anak Krakatau stands, Rita Susilawati of the PVMBG Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation told AFP . “Based on an evaluation of Sentinel satellite imagery, two formations resembling small islands can be seen around Mount Anak Krakatau” in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra islands, she added. Sentinel is a fleet of Earth observation spacecraft developed by the European Space Agency. One of the islands was located about 760 metres northwest of Mount Anak Krakatau, the other about 495 metres southwest. Rita said it was too early to refer to the islands as “children” of Mount Anak Krakatau — which itself was formed by an underwater eruption in the caldera or depression left behind after the massive 1883 blowout of the original Krakatau volcano. “Anak” means child in Bahasa Indonesia. Rita said further research was needed to determine if the new islands were emerging from the base of the caldera in a similar way than Anak Krakatau did, or whether they were formed by deposits of volcanic material. In the case of Anak Krakatau, several landmasses briefly emerged starting in 1927 and then disappeared due to erosion before an enduring island formed in 1930, she added. The two new islands may similarly be eroded away over time. Mount Anak Krakatau erupted for 25 hours non-stop in September, blanketing cities in volcanic ash and prompting multiple airports to close . More than 300,000 passengers were left stranded. Rita said Anak Krakatau was at alert Level 2, the second lowest out of four danger categories. People are advised not to approach within three kilometres (1.86 miles) of the eruption centre. Five journalists on a mission to cover the September eruption were declared presumed dead with three boat crew nearly two weeks after the vessel they were travelling in disappeared without trace. Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

Saudi Arabia denies reports of suicide bomber at Grand Mosque in Makkah. Saudi authorities on Friday denied reports of a suicide bomber at the Grand Mosque in Makkah, saying a man was arrested for harassing passersby and causing panic. “Security authorities in the holy capital arrested a person for harassing passersby and spreading fear and panic among them, and he was dealt with immediately,” authorities said in a statement on X. “The security authorities confirm that there is no truth to the claims being circulated regarding the incident,” the statement said. The statement provided no further details about the suspect. Taiwan's first new F-16V fighter jets arrive to bolster defences against China. The first two of a batch of 66 new ‌F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019 arrived in Taiwan on Friday after months of delays, helping to strengthen an air force that has to scramble almost daily to shadow China’s military. Taipei has complained of repeated delays to weapons ordered from the United States, its most ​important international backer and arms supplier. The delivery, to Taitung’s Chihhang Air Base on the island’s mountainous ⁠east coast, comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei, despite Washington saying there ​has been no change in policy. The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (0400 GMT or 9am PST). Speaking to reporters at ​parliament in Taipei shortly before, Defence Minister Wellington Koo said there would be other new F-16Vs arriving soon, though he did not give details. “Of course we won’t only have delivered these two by year-end,” he said. The United States in 2019 approved an $8 billion sale of Lockheed Martin F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan, a deal that would take the island’s F-16 fleet to more than 200 jets. But ​issues including software problems have delayed delivery of the planes. The arrival of the first two aircraft came almost exactly a week after US ‌President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington. Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing , that he was holding a new $14 billion package for Taiwan in abeyance, though he did approve one worth $11 billion in December 2025. A Lockheed Martin F-16V fighter jet lands at Taitung’s Chihhang Air Base in Taitung as people watch from a nearby hotel in Taitung, Taiwan, on October 2, 2026. — Reuters The F-16Vs have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters, though Washington has been unwilling ​to provide Taiwan its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35. An upgrade programme for ​Taiwan’s existing F-16s ⁠was completed in 2023. The United States is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations. Beijing has repeatedly told Washington to stop arming Taiwan. The Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to ⁠a request ​for comment on the arrival of the F-16s. “We continue standing with friends ​and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US State Department spokesperson said when asked about ​the new F-16s.

TTAP invites JI to multiparty moot, urges political parties to hold consultations. A delegation of the opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP), including Senate opposition leader Senator Allama Raja Nasir Abbas and PTI leaders, on Friday invited Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman to participate in a multiparty conference proposed by the opposition alliance. The opposition had first announced its intention to hold MPC on Sept 11, with the PTI leading the initiative. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan had outlined plans to hold the conference, saying that “the current law and order situation, the economy, inflation, lawlessness, and the creation of new provinces issue” called for such measures. On Friday, the delegation met the JI chief and discussed the country’s overall political situation, democratic process, supremacy of the Constitution and other national issues, according to a statement shared by TTAP on social media platform X. The statement said the participants stressed the “need to make communication and consultation among democratic and political forces more effective to promote political stability, strengthen democratic traditions and ensure the supremacy of the Constitution and law”. The participants agreed that dialogue and cooperation among political parties was essential for safeguarding national interests, democratic values and constitutional supremacy, it added. In a separate meeting, under the leadership of Senator Abbas, a TTAP delegation met former prime minister and Chairman of the Awam Pakistan Party Shahid Khaqan Abbasi at his residence. “During the meeting, a detailed exchange of views took place on the country’s overall political situation, the democratic process, the supremacy of the Constitution, and national issues,” the statement said. The delegation also invited Abbasi to participate in the MPC organised under the auspices of TTAP, it added. On the occasion, TTAP Vice Chairman and former senator Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar, as well as TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmad Yousafzai, were also present. “The meeting emphasised the need to continue the process of communication and consultation among all political forces for political stability in the country, the promotion of democratic traditions, and the supremacy of the Constitution,” the statement said. Barrister Gohar had announced the multiparty moot last month after a meeting with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) leaders, who have also agreed to attend the opposition’s moot. Earlier this week, the opposition alliance also invited PPP to attend the multiparty moot, which the ruling ally welcomed. Speaking to Dawn earlier this week, TTAP spokesperson Yousafzai said the MPC would be held after PTI’s protest, which is scheduled for Oct 4 to demand the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan. The TTAP has also formed a six-member committee to hold consultations with political parties and reach an agreement on the agenda for the proposed MPC. The development also comes as the federal government is set to hold talks with the opposition ahead of the October 4 protest. ‘All parties must consult’ Speaking at a joint media talk after the meetings, Abbas said all political parties had a responsibility to sit together and consult on the current situation in Pakistan. “All the parties that have a history in Pakistan, in forming and writing the Constitution, all the parties which might be in opposition or otherwise, it is their responsibility to sit and do mutual consultations and discuss this current situation in Pakistan, including the lackings in peace, politics, and economics, and take Pakistan out of it,” he said. “We met Hafiz Naeem today, grateful to him. Right now, there is an agenda for the All Parties Conference. Political parties should sit and discuss Pakistan’s problems, do an assessment of all the problems and then find a way out for all that,” he said. The senator said the current situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, particularly over the imposition of governor rule and emergency ahead of PTI’s October 4 protest call, also came under discussion during the meeting. “On that, we have consensus that there should not be an emergency,” he said, adding that he was grateful to Hafiz Naeem for speaking against emergency and governor’s rule. “These things will not strengthen Pakistan but instead further destabilise it and Pakistan will have more crises,” he said. He said Barrister Gohar and PTI leaders Salman Akram Raja, Amir Dogar, Haleem Adil Sheikh and Asad Qaiser were also part of the delegation. “I believe if all parties meet like this, we can take Pakistan out of crisis. They have the ability, the potential. Earlier also, whenever they’ve stepped into the field, they’ve given solutions, shown the way,” he said. Meanwhile, JI chief thanked Abbas and the other members of the delegation, saying the two sides had held a “good discussion”. “As far as the All Parties Conference is concerned, JI accepts this invitation and [..] we will take part,” he said, adding that “a national agenda right now is necessary” and “urgently needed”. He said the agenda should cover law and order, the economic situation and the rights of the people, with political forces reaching consensus on these issues. “We work along with the people to recover Pakistan so the country can move forward and progress,” he said. Rehman said the division of people into groups, with the perception that only a certain group could rule while the same people governed the economy, society and politics and the common people remained on the other side, needed to end. “That is why it is important to sit and discuss, come to a common ground, which is why I appreciate this,” he said. On the governor’s rule in KP and the proposal for an emergency in the province, Rehman said JI had opposed such measures in the past as well. “JI will not accept anything that suspends or disregards the Constitution or ruins any running system to achieve certain agendas. Any steps taken for it, JI will not support,” he said. “We don’t accept governor’s rule in KP . Similarly, we will not accept emergency under any conditions, and we oppose it,” he added. Rehman said the government should have held consultations and talks with the opposition earlier over PTI’s demands, adding that the delay had further deteriorated the situation. “Now that a committee has been formed, I consider it a good thing, but it should be meaningful instead of just sitting and doing a photo session,” he said. “It should reach a conclusion.” On PTI’s demands, he said they were “straightforward”, arguing that PTI founder was in jail and party members were unable to meet him. “This is not acceptable under any circumstances. They should be given access to meet,” he said. Regarding speculation about Imran’s health, Rehman said all concerns should be addressed, regardless of political differences. “Even if there is a political opponent, even then, considering that he is a human and an important political personality, ex-premier, how can this be ignored?” he said. “All the reservations regarding his health should be addressed, and the Supreme Court’s decision should be implemented in its spirit,” he said, referring to the SC’s August 18 order directing Imran’s transfer to a private medical facility. Rehman said PTI’s demands were “reasonable”, particularly those concerning the arrest of Imran’s sisters and Dr Yasmin Rashid, whom he described as unwell.

Lahore ranked as the most polluted city in the world, again. Lahore has once again emerged as the most polluted city in the world, with its air quality classified as “unhealthy”, according to air quality monitoring platform IQAir , as Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the government was making efforts to address environmental issues. In the past few years, air pollution has become one of the most pressing public health and environmental crises facing Pakistan. Various cities of the country, most notably Lahore , deal with smog, especially in the winter months. The phenomenon is attributed mainly to industrial emissions, vehicular pollution , stubble burning and air movement . Lahore topped the list of the most polluted cities on Friday morning, with an air quality index (AQI) of 167, according to the IQAir live tracker, falling under the ‘unhealthy’ category, closely followed by Bangladesh’s Dhaka at 164 and Egypt’s Cairo at 158. Figure shows the top ranked polluted cities according to IQAir on Friday morning. — Screengrab via IQAir Later in the day, Lahore’s ranking in the list of the world’s most polluted cities dropped to 10th, with an AQI of 149 at 2:00pm. The provincial capital was the only Pakistani city ranking in the top 30 most polluted cities on Friday morning. The only other Pakistani city in the 125-city list was Karachi at 34th place with an AQI of 69, on Friday morning. Later in the day, Karachi moved up a few spots to number 23 with an AQI of 75, as of 2:00pm. According to IQAir, in Lahore , “PM2.5 concentration is currently 15.2 times the World Health Organisation annual PM2.5 guideline value”. PM2.5 refers to fine inhalable particles, with diameters generally 2.5 micrometres and smaller. Of all air pollution measures, PM2.5 pollution poses the greatest health threat, according to IQAir. According to the website, PM2.5 can enter the circulatory system and even the brain, causing serious health complications if long-term exposure occurs. For those in Lahore, IQAir recommended avoiding outdoor exercise, closing windows to avoid outdoor air, wearing a mask outdoors and installing an air purifier indoors. Lahore air quality map. —IQAir Meanwhile, in a televised address to senior officers in Lahore on Friday, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said the provincial government was making efforts to address environmental issues. For the past eight years, she said, Lahore as well as some parts of Punjab would undergo a “smog shutdown” in September and October “For three years now — I won’t say there is zero smog, but — there is less smog,” she said. In January this year, Lahore was ranked as the most polluted city globally by IQAir with an AQI of 452. Earlier this week, a new analysis released by the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) ranked Lahore among cities whose ozone levels were “extremely poor”.

4 Pakistani crew members from hijacked oil tanker to arrive in Karachi tomorrow: DPM Dar. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Friday that four of the 10 Pakistani crew members of MT Honour 25 , an oil tanker hijacked by Somali pirates, had been “safely retrieved” and were scheduled to arrive in Karachi on Oct 3. The four crew members — Yasir Khan, Aqeel Khan, Amin bin Shams and Usman Ghani — were retrieved following “sustained efforts” by the Foreign Office (FO) and Pakistan’s embassy in Djibouti, Dar said. Meanwhile, the “mortal remains” of three Pakistani crew members — Rafi Ullah Khan, Syed Kashif Umer and Mahmood Ahmed Ansari — who “tragically” lost their lives were also being repatriated to Pakistan. “All necessary legal and other formalities [were] being fast-tracked to expedite the process,” Dar said, adding: “My heartfelt condolences go to the bereaved families, who are going through a deeply painful time.” The remaining three Pakistani crew members — Imran Ali, Yasin Muhammad and Syed Yousuf Hussain — remain aboard the vessel, along with the captain, Dar said. “We are actively coordinating with our friendly countries to facilitate their safe extraction and earliest possible return to Pakistan,” he said. Dar said the Foreign Affairs Ministry, under Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s leadership, “remains fully seized of the matter” and was continuously making every effort to ensure the return of all Pakistani nationals, including the bodies of the deceased, at the earliest. The ministry, he added, would continue extending “all possible support” to the affected families. Armed pirates hijacked the oil tanker off the southeastern coast of Somalia on April 21. For­eign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi had said the vessel, which was transporting oil to Somalia’s semi-autonomous Puntland reg­io­­n, had 17 crew members on board, including 10 Pakistanis. Somali maritime police on Sept 29 had recovered the Palau-flagged oil tanker amid reports of casualties among the crew. “The naval and ground units of the Puntland Maritime Police Force conducted a planned operation in the Dharin-Bar area of Bandar Beyla district,” the maritime police had said in its initial statement. In another statement, it announced that the operation had concluded and the recovered vessel “is now safe and under the Puntland government’s control”. During the operation, it said, 21 suspected pirates were apprehended, while operations to locate the remaining members continue. “Before the operation begun, the pirates on board the ship killed five of the crew. Among those killed were three from Pakistan, one from Myanmar and one from India,” it said. Reuters earlier reported, citing Puntland’s state television, that the detained pirates would be brought to court.

Asian Games: Pakistan settle for squash silver as Iran end volleyball run. Pakistan’s wait for a men’s squash team gold at the Asian Games goes on. Sixteen years after beating Malaysia 2-0 in Guangzhou for their last title in the event, Pakistan found the result reversed at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena on Friday, losing the final 2-0 to the same opponents and settling for silver — their second successive runners-up finish after also losing the final to India at the last edition in Hangzhou. Nasir Iqbal got the final under way against Ameeshenraj Chandaran and started brightly, racing into a 6-1 lead before Chandaran, ranked 95th in the world, clawed his way back into contention. The Malaysian cut the gap to 8-5 and then 9-7, but Nasir, ranked 94th, held his nerve to close out the opener 11-8 in nine minutes. Chandaran responded instantly in the second, surging from 4-2 to 10-2 with a six-point run before Nasir saved one game point but the 22-year-old converted his second opportunity to level the match at 11-3. The Malaysian carried that momentum into the third, trading points with Nasir up to 6-6 before reeling off four straight to reach game point and close it out 11-6, moving ahead in the match for the first time. Chandaran completed the job in the fourth, breaking clear from 5-3 with a five-point burst to reach match point and sealing an 11-4 win in nine minutes — a 3-1 victory in games that put Malaysia 1-0 up in the tie. That left Pakistan’s top-ranked Noor Zaman needing a win over Malaysia’s Eain Yow Ng to keep the final alive — the same opponent who had beaten him in the individual singles semi-final earlier in the Games, and the reigning singles gold medallist. The rematch went the full five games. Ng, ranked 18th in the world, built an early cushion to lead 9-4 before Noor rallied with three straight points, but the Malaysian held on to edge the opener 11-8 in nine minutes. Noor responded immediately in the second, tearing off four consecutive points from 3-3 to lead 7-3 and closing it out 11-6 to level the match. The third was the standout of the tie — a 15-minute war of long rallies in which neither player led by more than two points for long, before Noor edged clear late to win it 11-7 and move ahead 2-1. Ng hit back in ruthless fashion in the fourth, racing to a 5-0 lead and closing it out 11-4 in just five minutes to force a decider. The fifth game got away from Noor early. after a bright start, Ng took over, surging into a commanding lead and eventually sealing both the game and the gold for Malaysia with an 11-4 win in nine minutes. With Malaysia already 2-0 up, Pakistan’s third player, Mohammed Ashab Irfan — like Noor, a singles bronze medallist at these Games — did not need to take the court. Pakistan finish the men’s team event with silver, matching their result from 2022, as their search for a first Asian Games gold since 2010 continues. Iran halt Pakistan’s promising run Pakistan’s volleyball campaign will end with a shot at bronze after a 3-0 semi-final defeat to three-time defending champions Iran at the Okazaki Chuo Sogo Park Gymnasium on Friday. The scores were 25-13, 25-15, 25-11. Pakistan’s Ali Usman Faryad led the scoring with 11 points, while Murad Khan added nine and Afaq Khan chipped in with three. Jabran and Musawer Khan contributed two points apiece. Iran finished with 75 total points to Pakistan’s 39, and their dominance at the net was decisive — the Iranians converted 64 per cent of their spikes (43 of 68) compared to Pakistan’s 34 per cent (27 of 81), while also winning the blocking battle 15-1, a success rate of 32 per cent against Pakistan’s 4 per cent. Iran also edged the digs 64 per cent to 42 per cent. Pakistan had reached the last four with a commanding 3-0 quarter-final win over India, before falling to the hosts Japan in their final pool match. Pakistan will face either Japan or China in the bronze-medal match on Saturday. Iran, who had edged South Korea 3-2 in a five-set quarter-final thriller, advance to the final. Wrestling, taekwondo hopes dashed Pakistan’s Mohammad Abdullah fell in the men’s freestyle 65kg qualification on Friday, losing 13-2 to North Korea’s Kwang Jin Kim by technical superiority at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Centre. Kim, ranked No. 14 in the world at 65kg, needed just over two minutes to build an unassailable lead, ending the bout early under the 10-point mercy rule. In the men’s freestyle 86kg, Noman Zaka reached the quarter-finals with a 10-4 win over Cambodia’s Vuthy Heng before running into Japan’s Hayato Ishiguro, the 2025 World Championship silver medallist. Ishiguro won by technical superiority as Zaka failed to score. Noman then dropped into repechage, where Kazakhstan’s Azamat Dauletbekov — a two-time world bronze medallist and three-time Asian champion — also shut him out 10-0. At the Toyohashi Gymnasium, Shahzaib Khan lost a hard-fought taekwondo bout to Vietnam’s Hong Trong Nguyen, 2-1. Nguyen, a SEA Games gold medallist, edged the contest despite a determined effort from the Pakistani.

Hundreds of French high schools shut as new violence erupts. French high school students lit fires outside schools and faced off with police on Friday as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating. The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police. The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences. The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools — Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast — with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said. ‘Held hostage’ Education Minister Edouard Geffray said “the high school student movement is being held hostage by ultra-violent fringe groups,” adding that nearly 400 high schools out of the 3,700 in the country were expected to be closed on Friday. Many high schools have also planned to conduct classes remotely, particularly in the southern city of Marseille. At least 65 staff members have been injured, including 40 high school principals, since the start of the movement, Geffray told BFMTV . Some 170 students have been wounded while over 100 high schools have suffered “severe damage”. Dozens of people wearing face masks threw Molotov cocktails, torched trash bins and clashed with police. — AFP/File “Parents must clearly step up and tell their children not to go” to the protests, he added. “What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger.” Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said he has asked prosecutors to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children during the protests and “pay for repairs”. Since the start of the movement, around 2,000 people have been taken into police custody — 90 per cent of whom were minors“, Darmanin told RTL. ‘We’ve won’ In the western city of Rennes, the tension was already palpable outside the Jean-Mace high school with students dressed in black and wearing balaclavas standing not far from a heavy police presence. “As far as we’re concerned, we’ve won — our school is closed this morning,” said Lola, 16, who declined to give her last name. She condemned what she said was police violence. “It makes us even angrier — the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us.” Police used tear gas at the Kerichen high school in Brest, in western France, an AFP photographer said. The protests have also made a strong political echo just over half a year before presidential elections, with the government accusing the hard left France Unbowed (LFI) — whose firebrand leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is again standing for the presidency — of being behind the movement. But senior LFI official Manuel Bompard accused the government of “descending into conspiracy theories”. In a bid to ease tensions, Geffray said he was Friday meeting with education unions and high school student associations to find common ground for dialogue.

How the FCC is rolling back decades of progress through regressive jurisprudence. There is not a single woman judge on the Federal Constitutional Court. It is a court composed entirely of men. At the time of the 27th Amendment , various unconvincing justifications were presented: the amendments would reduce pendency of cases; “activist” judges had brought these changes upon themselves; the FCC would hear important cases of constitutional interpretation that consumed too much of the Supreme Court’s time. But it was clear then, and it is clear now. The courts were being stripped of their independence. This threatens far more than political cases. Once judicial independence is destroyed, no fundamental right is insulated from the consequences. Decades of legal advocacy have sought to strengthen protections for women. Regressive jurisprudence is undoing that work. The roll back of hard-won protections for women should concern everyone. Protections that took years to build are being dismantled. In its latest judgment, the FCC has restricted the scope of the workplace harassment law. The judgment was authored by Justice Ali Baqir Najafi. Justice Najafi is the same judge who wrote an additional note in Noor Mukadam’s case stating that the murder is a result of a “living [sic] relationships”, and that “the young generation must note its horrible consequences”. A judge who brought victim-blaming reasoning into the judicial treatment of a brutal murder has now authored a judgment that restricts the protections available under the workplace harassment law. Credit: Rida Hosain Restricting the definition of ‘harassment’ The FCC has adopted an interpretation of the workplace harassment law that undoes its very purpose. The FCC has held that only harassment that is “sexual in nature” is covered. The immediate consequence is that unless it can be shown that the conduct had a sexual element, it falls outside the protection of the law. This interpretation removes an important category of protection expressly included by parliament. The definition of harassment includes “sexually demeaning attitudes” when it interferes with work performance or creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive work environment. By reducing harassment to conduct that is “sexual in nature”, a wide range of gender-based abuse is placed outside the protection of the law. Humiliation, degrading treatment, intimidation, and a hostile work environment will no longer be recognised as harassment unless a sexual element can first be established. Justice Ayesha Malik previously held that reducing harassment to conduct that is sexual in nature “takes away the essence” of the harassment law, and ignores that harassment is often less about sexual interest and more about reinforcing existing power dynamics. Justice Ayesha held that the very “purpose of harassment laws is to address gender-based discrimination at the workplace and not to limit it to sexual forms of harassment”. Separately, Justice Mansoor Ali Shah, in Muhammad Din’s Case , made clear that harassment is not confined to conduct that is overtly sexual in nature. Speaking for the Court, Justice Shah held that “sexual harassment is not about sex. It is about power”, and recognised that discrimination on the basis of gender (whether sexual or non-sexual in nature) may constitute harassment where it reflects a discriminatory mindset and results in a hostile workplace. However, post the FCC judgment, a victim may be humiliated, degraded, intimidated or subjected to a hostile and discriminatory workplace, and yet be left without the protection of the workplace harassment law simply because the conduct cannot be characterised as sexual. In 2022, parliament amended the federal law, expressly broadening the definition of harassment to include “discrimination on the basis of gender, which may or may not be sexual in nature”. Sindh has adopted the federal law. To the extent the amendments apply, the judgment will only impact claims arising from conduct that occurred before the amendments came into force. The practical consequences of the FCC judgment will be most significant in Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan where the 2022 amendments do not apply. The responsibility now vests with the provincial legislatures to act without delay, and amend their respective workplace harassment laws to ensure that the protections parliament has recognised cannot be narrowed through regressive judicial interpretation. A legal framework that tells victims that gender-based abuse falls outside the harassment law unless it has a “sexual element” reinforces the culture of silence and impunity that the law was enacted to overcome. In a society where there is already severe underreporting, this judgment will deepen the silence. Increasing the evidentiary burden for victims The FCC held that to prove a sexual harassment, “a bare minimum requirement” is that “it must be reinforced with convincing/independent evidence”. The FCC seeks to impose a standard of proof that is detached from the realities of how harassment occurs. Workplace harassment often takes place in private settings through verbal comments, gestures, intimidation, or patterns of conduct that may not leave behind documentary or independent evidence. The reasoning suggests that a complainant’s own testimony is insufficient unless reinforced by independent material. The FCC’s approach creates an unjust hierarchy of evidence in which the direct testimony of a victim of harassment is treated as insufficient unless validated by independent evidence. Requiring independent corroboration sends a dangerous message that conduct behind closed doors may escape accountability. In our jurisprudence, in cases of gender-based violence, the courts have held that the sole testimony of a victim is sufficient if it is confidence inspiring and consistent. A victim experiencing harassment or coercive behaviour is often operating under conditions of shock, fear, and self-preservation. Expecting a victim to immediately assume the role of an investigator by recording conversations, collecting physical evidence, and preserving documents fundamentally misunderstands the realities of trauma and human behaviour. There is a fundamental distinction between assessing the credibility of a complainant’s testimony, and requiring the testimony to be corroborated by independent evidence. A court must assess whether a complaint is consistent, coherent, credible and to consider any surrounding circumstances. This is fundamentally different from treating independent evidence as a “bare minimum requirement” in harassment cases. Credit: Rida Hosain Even under the FCC’s narrow test, the allegations were sexual in character In the case before the FCC, the allegations were sexual, degrading, and coercive in character. In particular, it was alleged that the respondents: (i) Drew representations of female private parts with a marker on the glass of the desk, directed the complainant to identify them, and, when she refused, summoned male colleagues and asked them to explain the drawings to her in her presence. (ii) When the complainant wore loose clothing, one of the respondents threatened that he would tear off her clothes if she wore loose clothing again (a direct and explicit threat of physical and sexual violation). (iii) Compelled the complainant to remain in the office after working hours against her will (using his position and the workplace environment to exercise coercive control over her) (iv) Questioned the complainant about her marital status and whether she had a boyfriend (intruding into her private and intimate life in a manner directly relevant to the sexualised nature of the conduct alleged). These allegations include explicit depictions of female sexual anatomy, sexualised humiliation, a threat to forcibly remove the complainant’s clothing, intrusive questioning about her intimate relationships, and coercive conduct directed at her in the workplace. The question therefore bears asking: if alleged conduct of this nature is not “sexual in nature,” then what conduct is? The relevant question is one of legal characterisation. Whether the allegations were ultimately proved is a matter for the competent fact-finding forums to determine on the evidence. However, to frame the alleged conduct as non-sexual in nature is fundamentally flawed. Moreover, a substantial part of the FCC’s judgment rests on the principle that the High Court, in its constitutional jurisdiction, could not have interfered with or set aside the president’s order of censure. The decisive point was the limited scope of judicial review. To the extent the FCC’s observations were unnecessary for the disposal of the case, they ought to carry a different status. A legacy of regression The legacy the FCC is leaving behind is a legacy of regression from settled law as previously understood. This is not just about one case. In the Shahbaz Masih (2026) case , the FCC held that although child marriage is a criminal offence, the marriage itself would remain legally valid. The reasoning is deeply troubling particularly in its treatment of evidence concerning the child’s age. The Court disregarded documentary evidence and held: “these documents cannot be relied upon as the sole basis for concluding that Mst. Maria Bibi was born on 07.10.2012 as alleged by her father particularly when she is physically present in this court”, and “appears to be of a more advanced age”. The approach adopted by the FCC treats the apparent physical maturity of a girl as relevant to whether she should receive the legal protections afforded to a child. The FCC disregarded Nadra’s record and the birth certificate establishing the girl’s age as 12 years at the time of the alleged marriage, and instead placed reliance on her physical appearance. Rather than relying on documentary evidence, male judges were making their own subjective assessments about a minor girl’s age and maturity. The FCC’s jurisprudence reveals a clear unravelling of legal protections. Protections that took decades of legislative reform and advocacy to establish are being weakened by an all-male, executive-appointed court. The FCC is imposing a doctrine of regression across the entire judicial hierarchy. Editor’s Note: This article was temporarily taken offline for editorial review. It has been republished with only the addition of this phrase: “from settled law as previously understood”. The writer’s original headline has been retained as well.

First round of talks between govt, opposition end as PTI’s Oct 4 protest looms over federal capital. The first round of talks between the PTI-led opposition and the ruling coalition over the party’s proposed Oct 4 long march concluded on Friday, with both sides agreeing to resume the dialogue on Saturday. The meeting between government and opposition representatives, chaired by National Assembly Speaker Ayaz Sadiq, was aimed at defusing the country’s ongoing political crisis, with the PTI’s planned Oct 4 protest march demanding the release of party founder Imran Khan emerging as the latest point of contention between the party and the federal government. The PTI will formally present its demands to the government’s negotiating team on Saturday. The delegations apprised each other of their respective positions and held detailed discussions on various matters in a spirit of restraint, the National Assembly Secretariat said. According to the secretariat, the second round of talks will be held at 2pm on Saturday in the speaker’s chamber. It said the government and PPP had stressed the need to resolve national issues through negotiations with the opposition. The delegations were welcomed by Speaker Sadiq upon their arrival. “I am only playing the role of a mediator,” he said. Sadiq said his office was “always open” to resolving issues through negotiations and that he had consistently invited the opposition to engage in dialogue. He maintained that negotiations were the only way to resolve differences and issues, adding that positions and offices were temporary. “Parliament is the only forum where solutions to issues can be found,” he said. In an earlier post on X, the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) said negotiations with the government’s committee were underway, with the opposition side being led by the leader of the opposition in the Senate. Minister Amir Muqam, Adviser to the PM on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry and Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry attended the meeting, along with PPP Senator Sherry Rehman and National Assembly members Syed Naveed Qamar and Ejaz Hussain Jakhrani. The opposition was represented by PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan, Senate opposition leader Raja Nasir Abbas, Amir Dogar, former National Assembly speaker Asad Qaiser and PTI General Secretary Salman Akram Raja. As the PTI remains resolute to go ahead with the march, federal ministers have warned that the Centre would have no other option but to impose the governor’s rule or emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in light of the security situation in the province and the PTI’s protest call. For its part, the opposition party has warned the government of dire consequences if such a decision is imposed. Govt should engage opp ‘with integrity’ Senate Opposition Leader Senator Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, speaking to the media at his office during a break in talks with the government, said the government should engage with the opposition “with integrity” and take steps towards resolving the issues. “If the government cares about the political crisis, then it should sit with the opposition with integrity and step forward to find a solution,” he said. Regarding PTI’s long march, Senator Nasir said the call would remain “intact” until a solution was found. “Negotiating is the way of political leaders; negotiations could resolve gigantic issues and war,” he said, adding that “it, however, depends on the government’s intention”. He questioned whether the government, as the other party to the negotiations, genuinely wanted to resolve the issues. “They are in government and it is their responsibility to maintain peace, resolve crises, and ensure economic stability,” he said. Senator Nasir reiterated that the outcome depended on how “autonomous” the government was and whether it had the “intent” to pursue negotiations. A day earlier, it emerged that a joint delegation of the PPP and the government would hold a meeting with the PTI leadership on Friday, during which the “current political situation” in the country would be discussed with the opposition. The decision came after a meeting at the presidency attended by President Asif Ali Zardari, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, and other party leaders. Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah also said on Thursday that the federal government and PTI were engaged in “off-the-record talks” regarding PTI’s planned protest. Sanaullah said that the decision on the proposed march rested with PTI’s senior leadership, “with whom off-the-record consultation is ongoing”. “So let us see, even if they do not postpone it, we have arrangements in place to stop them,” he warned.

Cop martyred, another injured in attack on police in KP’s Tank district. DERA ISMAIL KHAN: A policeman was martyred and another injured when unidentified assailants targeted law enforcers deployed at a hospital in Jandola, a merged tehsil of Tank district, police said on Friday. According to police, the attackers opened fire and hurled a hand grenade at the policemen stationed at the hospital’s entrance before fleeing the scene. Police personnel reached the site and launched a search operation in the area following the attack, police said. Further details about the nature of the attack and the identities of the assailants were not immediately available. Earlier in the week, three traffic policemen were martyred when unidentified armed men opened fire on their mobile van in the Wazirabad Bazaar area of Tank district. The attackers had also taken away the traffic police vehicle after the incident. However, the vehicle was later recovered. This month, at least 21 people, including 15 police officials, were martyred when an explosives-laden vehicle detonated near a mosque in Kohat Police Lines, followed by terrorists storming the compound and attacking police facilities, according to senior police and district health officials. On July 26, a terrorist attack on a joint police checkpost in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Tank district martyred 15 people, including 14 security personnel, the military’s media wing. Among those martyred were 12 soldiers, two policemen and a government official.

Army's top brass warns of 'decisive force' against any 'May 9-like situation'. The army’s top brass on Friday warned that any attempt at creating agitation or a “May 9-like situation” would be dealt with “decisive force”, according to the military’s media wing. The warning came during the 277th Corps Commanders’ Conference in Rawalpindi, which was presided over by Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir. “[The] forum underscored the importance of internal stability and resolved that any attempt to cause agitation or create [a] May 9-like situation, on any pretext whatsoever, will be dealt with decisive force and rule of law, without hesitation and discrimination,” a statement from Inter-Services Public Relations said. The warning comes as the PTI is gearing up for a long march to Islamabad, to demand the release of former prime minister and party founder Imran Khan. The protest was originally scheduled for Sept 27 but was postponed to Oct 4. The party is currently in talks with the government over its long march, with the first round of dialogue taking place earlier in the day. It is worth mentioning that Imran’s arrest on May 9, 2023, had triggered widespread riots across Pakistan, during which government buildings and military installations — including the GHQ in Rawalpindi — were stormed and vandalised. Following the unrest, a crackdown was launched against the PTI, with dozens of terrorism cases lodged against its leaders and supporters. Need for ‘targeted action’ against Afghanistan stressed According to ISPR, the forum also reviewed the security landscape and resolved to maintain a “high state of readiness”. It hailed successful counter-terrorism operations, but stressed the need to blend kinetic and non-kinetic measures. These included “people-centric governance at [the] grassroot level, strategic engagement with [the] public, dismantling of [the] terror-crime nexus operating under patronage of vested interests and police capacity building, in line with the National Action Plan and Vision Azm-i-Istehkam”. Affirming Pakistan’s right to self-defence, the forum noted the need for “targeted action” against terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, stressing that “only the Taliban’s delusional leadership, facilitating terrorism on behalf of India, bears responsibility for its consequences”. Since Sep 21, in the aftermath of terror incidents in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan has carried out three strikes in Afghanistan, targeting terrorist hideouts. A day earlier, ISPR Director General Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said that Pakistan had the right to self-defence and “everything that is necessary will be done” in response to terrorism emanating from Afghanistan . Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia condemned The army huddle on Friday also welcomed the Makkah Defence Alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye and its contribution to “longstanding strategic and collective defence ties”, the statement read. “It (the forum) strongly resented Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, expressed solidarity with the kingdom and affirmed Pakistan’s commitment to the security and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain,” ISPR added. The defence pact , signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. Fresh fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Both sides have claimed strikes on each other as tensions remain high. The Corps Commander Conference on Friday also reiterated Pakistan’s position on Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir and expressed support for resolving the Kashmir dispute, in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people. The SPDC, established under the trilateral Makkah Accord, comprised of three members from each country, he noted: the foreign ministers, defence ministers and chiefs of army staff. On Sept 25, a special meeting took place of the three army chiefs in Riyadh, he said, adding that the foreign ministers had met before this in New York, on Sept 24, in the wake of increased Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. “Very soon, a meeting of the whole SPDC … has been agreed to in principle, to take place in Riyadh,” the deputy premier said, noting that the current situation and “ground reality” would be examined during the meeting, particularly vis-a-vis Saudi Arabia. He added that details of the meeting would be shared after it took place. Responding to a question, DPM Dar said that this upcoming meeting was an emergency one, and the committee would meet again as planned after “the end of October or beginning of November”, when its work was expected to be completed. The UN’s High Level Week, Secretary-General Selection and “Middle Power” Problem hschaub Fri, 09/18/2026 - 17:29 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Podcast / Global 18 September 2026 1 minute The UN’s High Level Week, Secretary-General Selection and “Middle Power” Problem This week on Hold Your Fire!, Richard Atwood is joined by Crisis Group experts Richard Gowan and Daniel Forti to discuss next week’s UN General Assembly high-level week and whether a new Secretary-General can revive the organisation’s peacemaking as global turmoil spreads. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy In this episode of Hold Your Fire! , Richard Atwood speaks with Richard Gowan, Crisis Group’s Director for Global Issues and Institutions, and Daniel Forti, Head of UN affairs, ahead of next week’s UN General Assembly high-level week. They explore the mood at the UN, its shifting relations with Washington and its shrinking role in peacemaking worldwide, particularly in the Middle East. They assess current Secretary-General António Guterres’s legacy, the contenders to succeed him and whether new leadership can reinvigorate the organisation’s peacemaking while defending the UN Charter’s principles and rebuilding relationships with powerful states. They also discuss how UN peacekeeping missions can adapt to fragile ceasefires and how much Western and non-Western mid-sized powers, which appear increasingly drawn to other forums, will invest in the UN’s future.
